articles.title: Lời khai ban đầu của nữ tài xế ô tô chèn ép, tông ngã thai phụ ở Lào Cai
articles.text:
TPO - Võ Tuyết S ( sinh năm 1990) khai nhận thời điểm đó đang lái xe ô tô di chuyển chở theo con trai, do không bật tín hiệu xi nhan chuyển hướng nên xảy ra mâu thuẫn với chị P.T.T đang đi xe máy điện trên đường. Hai bên sau đó đã xảy ra cãi vã.
Ngày 4/11, Công an phường Lào Cai cho biết, đơn vị đã tiến hành triệu tập người điều khiển ô tô đến làm việc để xác minh, làm rõ vụ việc liên quan đến đoạn video ghi lại cảnh ô tô có hành vi chèn ép, va chạm với xe máy điện trên đường Hoàng Liên, phường Lào Cai, tỉnh Lào Cai.
Trước đó, trên mạng xã hội facebook lan truyền đoạn clip ngắn ghi lại hình ảnh chiếc xe ô tô nhãn hiệu Vinfast VF3 màu hồng, biển kiểm soát 24A-376.xx liên tiếp chèn ép rồi va chạm với người phụ nữ điều khiển xe máy điện, gây bức xúc dư luận
Võ Tuyết S tại cơ quan công an.
Ngay sau tiếp nhận thông tin, Công an phường Lào Cai đã tiến hành triệu tập và làm việc với người điều khiển ô tô là Võ Tuyết S (SN 1990, trú tại tổ dân phố số 25 Kim Tân, phường Lào Cai).
Tại cơ quan Công an, S khai nhận: Khoảng 15h ngày 1/11, tại đường Hoàng Liên, thuộc tổ dân phố số 24 Kim Tân, phường Lào Cai, S điều khiển ô tô chở con trai lưu thông từ khu vực chung cư Tecco theo hướng cầu Kim Tân.
Khi di chuyển, do không bật tín hiệu xi nhan chuyển hướng nên xảy ra mâu thuẫn với chị P.T.T (SN 1990, trú tại phường Cam Đường) điều khiển xe máy điện. Sau khi hai bên lời qua tiếng lại, S đã có hành vi điều khiển phương tiện áp sát, chèn ép xe máy điện, không cho chị P.T.T di chuyển về phía trước.
Có thời điểm, chiếc ô tô đánh lái, quay ngang trên đường, chắn một phần lối lưu thông. Khi chị P.T.T điều khiển xe vượt lên và dừng tại khu vực đèn đỏ, ô tô tiếp tục tiến lên áp sát xe máy điện, sau đó va chạm vào phần đuôi xe máy điện của chị P.T.T khiến chiếc xe máy điện bị đổ ra đường. Chị P.T.T được xác định đang mang thai và được điều trị tại Bệnh viện sản nhi tỉnh Lào Cai.
Chị T bị xe ô tô nhãn hiệu VinFast VF3 tông vào đuôi xe. Ảnh cắt từ clip.
Tại cơ quan Công an, Võ Tuyết S thừa nhận hành vi đánh lái, chèn ép xe máy điện, cản trở việc di chuyển của chị P.T.T. Võ Tuyết S khai, việc chèn ép xe máy điện xuất phát từ sự bức xúc khi hai bên xảy ra cãi vã và muốn tiếp tục tranh luận với người phụ nữ đi xe máy.
Hiện Công an phường Lào Cai đang tiếp tục xác minh, thu thập tài liệu, làm rõ toàn bộ diễn biến vụ việc, đánh giá tính chất, mức độ hành vi của những người liên quan để xử lý theo quy định của pháp luật.
TPO - "Đá" được chuẩn bị sẵn, kết quả tìm thấy "ngọc" do nhóm tổ chức ra tín hiệu để người dẫn livestream thông báo. Với thủ đoạn này, các bị cáo cùng đồng phạm đã chiếm đoạt hơn 263,9 tỷ đồng của nạn nhân.
TPO - Trong quá trình truy bắt hai đối tượng tàng trữ trái phép chất ma túy trên Tỉnh lộ 108, hai cán bộ CSGT Công an tỉnh Sơn La đã bị các đối tượng cắn vào cánh tay. Qua xác minh, cả hai đối tượng đều nhiễm HIV.
TPO - Đột kích căn biệt thự sang trọng tại phường Điện Bàn Đông (TP Đà Nẵng), công an phát hiện 13 người nước ngoài tổ chức đường dây lừa đảo xuyên quốc gia. Nhóm này sử dụng 87 điện thoại, 12 máy tính để giăng bẫy tình cảm, dụ các nạn nhân ở Indonesia chuyển tiền đầu tư rồi chiếm đoạt.
TPO - Công an tỉnh Lào Cai đã khởi tố, bắt tạm giam Lý A Lềnh (SN 1985, trú xã Mường Khương) về tội Giết người sau khi đối tượng dùng dao chém 3 người thân bị thương rồi bỏ trốn.
TPO - Theo luật sư, khi chưa đăng ký kết hôn, hai người chưa phát sinh nghĩa vụ chung thủy theo pháp luật hôn nhân và gia đình. Việc ghen tuông không đồng nghĩa có quyền xâm phạm đời tư, quay và phát tán clip nhạy cảm của người yêu.
TPO - Mặc dù khu vực mà Hồ Văn Tình kịp chạy thoát thời điểm bắt được Lữ Văn Toàn sáng 3/11 là rừng núi thôn Cây Cày (xã Bắc Khánh Vĩnh, tỉnh Khánh Hòa), nhưng hiện nơi lực lượng truy bắt đang tập trung vây ráp truy lùng phạm nhân Tình lại là núi Hòn Dữ-khu vực có địa hình cực kỳ hiểm trở.
TPO - Viện Kiểm sát cho biết, sẽ tiếp tục điều tra trong giai đoạn 2 của vụ án để làm rõ hành vi của hơn 1.400 người khác trong bộ máy do Phó Đức Nam điều hành; hoạt động của các cổng trung gian thanh toán như BigPay, ApotaPay, CPay.
TPO - Hơn 4,4 tấn hải sâm được đưa từ Lào vào Quảng Trị qua đường tiểu ngạch, dự kiến chuyển cho đầu mối chế biến, bán kiếm lời. Công an đã khởi tố 4 bị can liên quan.
TPO - 5 bị can trong vụ án liên quan Ngân hàng SCB được Viện KSND Tối cao kêu gọi ra đầu thú, để thực hiện quyền bào chữa và hưởng chính sách khoan hồng.
TPO - Quá trình bóc gỡ đường dây ma tuý số lượng lớn có nguồn gốc từ Campuchia, Công an TP Hà Nội đã bắt giữ 137 đối tượng, thu giữ hơn 39kg ma túy các loại cùng súng, đạn và nhiều tang vật liên quan.
TPO - Nhận tiền để giúp doanh nghiệp xin xuất khẩu quặng sắt, cựu Phó giám đốc một công ty dịch vụ du lịch đã tìm gặp ông Nguyễn Văn Vịnh (thời điểm đó là Bí thư Tỉnh ủy Lào Cai), rồi tiếp xúc với lãnh đạo UBND tỉnh và Sở Công Thương, để giúp doanh nghiệp được xuất khẩu quặng ra nước ngoài.
TPO - Công an Tây Ninh phát hiện 26 vụ với 55 đối tượng liên quan hoạt động xuất nhập cảnh trái phép, trong đó nhiều người bị dụ sang Campuchia bằng chiêu “việc nhẹ, lương cao”.
TPO - Công an tỉnh An Giang vừa triệt phá đường dây mua bán, sử dụng trái phép ma túy, khởi tố 6 đối tượng và thu giữ 740 gam ma túy tổng hợp cùng nhiều tang vật, trong đó có súng, đạn và lựu đạn.
TPO - Ngày 4/11, Cục An ninh mạng (Bộ Công an) đưa ra khuyến cáo liên quan đến các đoạn clip ghi lại vụ mâu thuẫn tình cảm, bắt ghen được cho là xảy ra tại xã Tân An Hội, TP.HCM. Theo đó, hành vi phát tán dữ liệu cá nhân nhằm bôi nhọ, xúc phạm danh dự, nhân phẩm có thể dẫn đến trách nhiệm pháp lý, thậm chí bị truy cứu trách nhiệm hình sự.

articles.title: Thẻ ETC bị thu hồi sau giao dịch, lộ bất thường trong thanh toán phí cao tốc
articles.text:
18 phương tiện phát sinh giao dịch rồi thu hồi thẻ
Tổng công ty Đầu tư phát triển đường cao tốc Việt Nam (VEC) vừa có văn bản gửi Cục Đường bộ Việt Nam, đề nghị phối hợp kiểm tra, xử lý và tăng cường các giải pháp phòng ngừa hành vi gian lận trong thanh toán điện tử giao thông đường bộ.
Động thái này được đưa ra sau khi VEC ghi nhận một số trường hợp phương tiện lưu thông trên tuyến cao tốc Đà Nẵng - Quảng Ngãi có dấu hiệu bất thường trong quá trình sử dụng dịch vụ thu phí điện tử.
Theo VEC, qua báo cáo của Công ty Cổ phần TASCO - đơn vị tổ chức thu phí trên tuyến, trong thời gian từ ngày 9/10 - 18/10/2026, hệ thống ghi nhận 11 lượt phương tiện lưu thông qua trạm thu phí Dung Quất nhưng không nhận diện được Etag hoặc camera không quan sát được biển số cố định. Trong số này, có 7 lượt phương tiện không rõ biển số và 4 lượt sử dụng biển số tạm nhưng có dấu hiệu không đủ điều kiện.
Một vấn đề khác được VEC đặc biệt lưu ý là tình trạng sử dụng biển số tạm, sau đó thu hồi thẻ Etag khi giao dịch đã phát sinh.
Theo báo cáo của TASCO, qua rà soát danh sách giao dịch cần xử lý sau khi kết nối liên thông tuyến cao tốc đầu tư công, đơn vị ghi nhận 22 giao dịch liên quan đến 18 phương tiện, tương ứng 18 Etag.
Các giao dịch phát sinh trong khoảng thời gian từ ngày 6/9 - 6/10/2026. Phương tiện vào cao tốc bằng hình thức thu phí đầu vào tại trạm Dung Quất nhưng không được ghi nhận thu phí đầu ra, sau đó di chuyển tiếp sang tuyến cao tốc đầu tư công.
Qua kiểm tra, các thẻ Etag trong danh sách đã chuyển trạng thái thu hồi. Điều này khiến TASCO không thể thực hiện truy thu phí sử dụng đường bộ đối với những giao dịch đã phát sinh.
Tổng số tiền chưa thu được và đang tiếp tục xử lý là gần 16 triệu đồng. Trong đó, 19 giao dịch tại trạm Túy Loan với số tiền hơn 14.700.000 đồng; một giao dịch tại Phong Thử với số tiền hơn 471.000 đồng; một giao dịch tại Chu Lai với số tiền hơn 147.000 đồng và một giao dịch tại Hà Lam với số tiền gần 573.000 đồng.
TASCO cho biết qua công tác quản lý, vận hành và hậu kiểm giao dịch thu phí trên tuyến Đà Nẵng - Quảng Ngãi, đơn vị phát hiện nhiều lượt phương tiện có dấu hiệu không bảo đảm điều kiện lưu thông, không có biển số hoặc sử dụng biển số tạm, thẻ ETC không hợp lệ. Một số trường hợp phương tiện có dấu hiệu tác động vào thẻ và sử dụng thẻ không đủ điều kiện.
VEC nhận định đây là hình thức có dấu hiệu lợi dụng quy trình quản lý Etag, tài khoản giao thông nhằm né tránh nghĩa vụ thanh toán.
Siết quy trình thu hồi thẻ ETC, tránh thất thoát phí cao tốc
Từ những bất thường trên, VEC đề nghị Cục Đường bộ Việt Nam hỗ trợ chỉ đạo các nhà cung cấp dịch vụ ETC đối soát, truy xuất lịch sử sử dụng Etag, đặc biệt đối với các thẻ đã chuyển trạng thái thu hồi sau khi phát sinh giao dịch, nhằm xác định phương tiện gắn thẻ tại thời điểm giao dịch và xử lý số tiền dịch vụ sử dụng đường bộ chưa thu.
Đồng thời, VEC kiến nghị rà soát quy trình khóa, thu hồi, thay thế hoặc chấm dứt hiệu lực Etag, bảo đảm việc thay đổi trạng thái thẻ không làm mất khả năng truy xuất dữ liệu, lịch sử giao dịch và xác định nghĩa vụ thanh toán đã phát sinh trước đó.
Một nội dung đáng chú ý khác là đề xuất nghiên cứu cơ chế cảnh báo đối với những trường hợp thẻ Etag phát sinh giao dịch chưa thanh toán nhưng chưa có yêu cầu khóa hoặc thu hồi; biển số camera nhận diện không trùng khớp với biển số gắn với tài khoản giao thông; hoặc phương tiện có giao dịch chưa được xử lý nhưng tiếp tục xuất hiện tại các điểm thu khác.
Theo VEC, việc cảnh báo cần được thực hiện trên cơ sở dữ liệu dùng chung và bảo đảm các quy định về bảo mật, bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân.
VEC đề nghị Cục Đường bộ Việt Nam hướng dẫn và phối hợp xử lý, đồng thời xem xét các giải pháp phòng ngừa để những tình huống tương tự không tiếp tục phát sinh.

articles.title: Top 25 Hoa hậu Việt Nam 2026 rèn bản lĩnh trả lời ứng xử
articles.text: Trước đêm chung kết, Top 25 Hoa hậu Việt Nam 2026 được trang bị kiến thức văn hóa, xã hội và rèn luyện kỹ năng ứng xử. Không chỉ là phần thi quan trọng, ứng xử còn là dịp để các thí sinh thể hiện tư duy, bản lĩnh và góc nhìn trước những vấn đề của đời sống.

articles.title: Kết quả cuộc tình khiến Lisa bị mạt sát
articles.text:
Tờ Thairath đưa tin nam diễn viên Blue Pongtiwat vừa tham gia một sự kiện quảng bá cho bộ phim Hoàng hậu tái hôn, trực tiếp phủ nhận đang hẹn hò với Lisa (Black Pink).
Nam diễn viên sinh năm 2000 khẳng định chỉ là bạn thân với Lisa. Cả hai cùng ở trong một nhóm bạn nên thường đi chơi và ủng hộ nhau, nhưng chưa chạm tới ngưỡng yêu đương như công chúng đồn đoán lâu nay.
Blue Pongtiwat cho biết những lần hợp tác trước đây của hai người là trong dự án dẫn chương trình của Tổng Cục Du lịch Thái Lan. Nam nghệ sĩ khẳng định anh còn độc thân, không hẹn hò với ai. Blue Pongtiwat cũng phủ nhận việc thất nghiệp, phải ăn bám Lisa suốt thời gian qua.
"Khi thấy những ồn ào trên tin tức, tôi vẫn cứ sống như bình thường thôi, chẳng thấy căng thẳng gì cả. Bởi tôi và chị Lisa khá thân thiết vì bạn bè của tôi và ê-kíp của chị ấy đều thuộc cùng một nhóm bạn", Blue Pongtiwat giải thích về mối quan hệ với Lisa.
"Thời gian gần đây tôi đang tận hưởng cuộc sống và cũng cố gắng nhiều trong công việc. Tôi đang chuẩn bị nhạc, sẽ sớm gửi tới để mọi người thưởng thức", nam ca sĩ phủ nhận việc bám vào danh tiếng của Lisa.
Mối quan hệ giữa Lisa và Blue Pongtiwat được chú ý từ đầu năm 2026, khi nam diễn viên Thái Lan xuất hiện trong tiệc sinh nhật lần thứ 29 của nữ ca sĩ. Blue sau đó đăng ảnh chụp thân thiết cùng Lisa tại bãi biển, kèm lời chúc sinh nhật.
Từ đó, cả hai liên tục bị đặt nghi vấn đi cùng nhau tại Thái Lan, Hong Kong (Trung Quốc) và Nhật Bản. Một số nguồn tin còn cho rằng Blue từng gặp gỡ gia đình Lisa. Hồi tháng 8, hai bên gia đình Lisa - Blue Pongtiwat cùng tổ chức sinh nhật muộn cho mẹ Blue.
Đến tháng 9, Lisa và Blue Pongtiwat cùng đăng ảnh check-in tại Nhật Bản khiến dân mạng xôn xao. Ngày 15/10, Lisa lại được trông thấy ngồi cạnh "bạn trai tin đồn" tại một nhà hàng ở Bangkok.
Tin đồn Lisa hẹn hò Blue nhận phản ứng trái chiều. Một bộ phận ủng hộ mối quan hệ này. Họ cho rằng Lisa đã 29 tuổi, có quyền yêu đương và tận hưởng đời sống riêng tư.
Nhưng cũng có những cư dân mạng tỏ ra gay gắt vì suy đoán Lisa "mập mờ" với Blue khi đang hẹn hò với doanh nhân Pháp Frédéric Arnault. Một số khác cáo buộc Blue “dựa hơi” Lisa và không xứng với người đẹp sinh năm 1997.
Lisa cũng bị mắng mải mê yêu đương mà bỏ bê BlackPink cũng như người hâm mộ. Có người nhắc lại thái độ hời hợt của ngôi sao Rockstar trong dịp kỷ niệm 10 năm BlackPink ra mắt, chỉ dành chút ít thời gian ở cùng nhóm và giao lưu fan, rồi bay sang Nhật Bản để hội ngộ Blue.
Blue Pongtiwat Tangwancharoen sinh ngày 15/3/2000, kém Lisa ba tuổi. Anh bước vào ngành giải trí từ khi còn nhỏ, được biết tới qua các phim như Krong Kam, Leh Game Rak, You are My Heartbeat, The Family và đặc biệt là Ready, Set, Love của Netflix. Theo South China Morning Post, anh là nghệ sĩ đa năng, từng học ngành điện ảnh và truyền thông kỹ thuật số tại Đại học Srinakharinwirot (Thái Lan).
Blue đang phát triển sự nghiệp âm nhạc. Năm 2026, anh hợp tác với nam ca sĩ Thái Lan TEN trong dự án âm nhạc You Give Me Butterflies. Tháng 8, anh ra mắt ca khúc solo Kiss, Come Kiss dưới sự quản lý của LOVEiS Entertainment.
Blue sở hữu ngoại hình ưa nhìn với chiều cao 1,83 m. Một số phương tiện truyền thông gọi anh là “Cha Eun Woo của Thái Lan”. Tuy nhiên, nếu so về độ nổi tiếng và giàu có, Blue khó lòng sánh bằng Lisa - một ngôi sao quốc tế.

articles.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
articles.text:
A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Kyushu University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.
- Share:
Muscles can begin losing their strength and ability to recover surprisingly early in the aging process. Over time, muscle tissue may develop scar tissue, accumulate fat, and lose some of the specialized fibers responsible for rapid, powerful movements. These changes can make everyday activities more difficult and gradually reduce mobility and physical independence.
Now, scientists in Japan have identified a promising molecule that could help protect the body's natural muscle repair system and potentially make it more effective. In laboratory experiments, the compound strengthened an important biological signal involved in muscle regeneration, increasing its ability to connect with a key cellular receptor by more than twofold.
The discovery comes from a team led by Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi at Kyushu University's Faculty of Agriculture. Their findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest a possible new approach to addressing the cellular changes that make aging muscles increasingly difficult to repair.
How Aging Disrupts the Body's Muscle Repair System
Skeletal muscles are the muscles attached to bones that allow us to walk, lift objects, maintain posture, and perform other voluntary movements. Although these muscles experience wear and tear throughout life, they also have a remarkable ability to repair themselves.
Much of that repair depends on specialized stem cells known as satellite cells. These cells normally remain inactive, positioned alongside muscle fibers until they receive a signal that repair or regeneration is needed. Once activated, they can multiply and develop into muscle cells that help restore damaged tissue.
An essential part of this process involves a protein called hepatocyte growth factor, or HGF. Despite its name, HGF plays important roles beyond the liver, including helping activate the stem cells responsible for muscle regeneration.
Under normal conditions, HGF is stored within the supportive material surrounding muscle fibers. When muscles experience an injury or mechanical stimulation, such as physical movement or stretching, the protein can be released.
HGF then attaches to a receptor called c-met on the surface of satellite cells. Receptors are specialized proteins that receive molecular signals and trigger responses inside cells. In this case, the interaction helps awaken dormant satellite cells, allowing them to multiply, mature, and participate in repairing muscle fibers.
But this carefully coordinated system becomes less reliable with age.
A Hidden Chemical Change May Weaken Aging Muscles
The researchers' previous work revealed that HGF can undergo a chemical modification known as nitration. This process attaches a chemical group called a nitro group to particular locations on a protein, potentially changing its structure and interfering with its normal activity.
For HGF, the researchers identified two especially important locations, Y198 and Y250. Both lie within the region involved in attaching to the c-met receptor.
When these sites undergo nitration, HGF becomes less capable of connecting with its receptor. The result is similar to a key that has become damaged and can no longer operate its intended lock.
This disruption could have important consequences for aging muscles. Even if the body continues producing HGF, chemical changes may prevent the protein from properly activating the stem cells needed for tissue repair. The researchers believe this mechanism may contribute to age-related muscle wasting and declining regenerative capacity.
"HGF is not necessarily missing as we age," explains Tatsumi. "Rather, it can be chemically altered after it is made. That led us to wonder whether a compound with strong antioxidant capacity might protect HGF, either by preventing nitration or by compensating for the functional loss it causes."
Scientists Test Two Powerful Sulfur Compounds
To investigate that possibility, the team studied two compounds with strong antioxidant properties: glutathione trisulfide (GSSSG) and lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS).
Antioxidants can help limit certain types of chemical damage caused by reactive molecules. Such damage can interfere with proteins and other essential components of cells, particularly when the body's normal protective systems become less effective.
The two compounds belong to a chemical family called trisulfides. Their defining feature is a chain of three sulfur atoms connected to one another. This arrangement gives them unusual chemical properties, including an ability to participate in reactions involving the transfer of electrons, known as redox reactions.
Because these reactions play important roles in cellular chemistry, trisulfides have attracted growing interest as potential ingredients in new medicines.
In the first set of experiments, both compounds reduced nitration at the two vulnerable sites on HGF. However, preventing this chemical modification did not completely restore the protein's ability to attach to c-met.
The scientists therefore increased the amount of trisulfide used relative to HGF. They changed the molar ratio, which compares the number of molecules of each substance, from 1:4000 to 1:8000.
That adjustment produced an unexpected result.
An Unexpected Discovery Creates "Super HGF"
At the higher concentration, LASSS did much more than protect HGF from chemical damage. It also dramatically improved the protein's ability to bind to its receptor.
Compared with untreated HGF, the protein exposed to LASSS showed more than twice the binding affinity for c-met. In other words, it could attach to its target receptor much more strongly, potentially enhancing a critical step in the muscle repair process.
The treatment also made HGF more resistant to the loss of function caused by nitration, particularly at the Y198 site.
Notably, the effect was specific to LASSS. Although GSSSG had also reduced nitration in the earlier experiments, it did not produce the same improvement in receptor binding.
"This exceeded our expectations," comments Tatsumi. "We knew trisulfides had diverse biological functions, but we never expected that simply mixing HGF with LASSS would produce such a striking effect.
"What this tells us is that LASSS does more than simply neutralize reactive molecules. It may interact directly with HGF and induce a subtle structural change, creating an enhanced 'Super HGF' form that binds c-met more strongly and resists nitration."
The researchers suspect that LASSS interacts with HGF in a way that slightly alters the protein's three-dimensional shape. Because a protein's shape helps determine how well it interacts with other molecules, even a small structural adjustment could substantially change its activity.
The result is what the team describes as "Super HGF," a potentially enhanced form of the body's existing muscle repair signal.
Importantly, stronger receptor binding does not automatically establish that muscle regeneration itself has improved. Additional experiments will be needed to determine whether this molecular enhancement translates into better muscle healing and strength.
Mouse Experiments Reveal Promising Protection
After observing the effects in laboratory experiments, the researchers wanted to determine whether LASSS could also protect HGF inside living muscle tissue.
They used mice subjected to tail suspension, an established experimental method for studying muscle atrophy. By reducing normal weight bearing and muscle use, this technique produces some of the changes associated with prolonged inactivity, including muscle deterioration.
Mice that received LASSS before the experiment showed significantly less HGF nitration than untreated animals. This suggested that the compound's ability to protect the muscle repair protein was not limited to controlled laboratory conditions.
Once again, GSSSG failed to produce the same protective result.
These findings provide early evidence that LASSS can influence the chemical processes affecting HGF within living animals. However, the mouse experiments demonstrated protection against nitration, not that LASSS restored lost muscle mass or improved physical strength.
The researchers emphasize that studies involving aging animals are still necessary to establish the compound's effectiveness and safety in vivo, meaning within a living organism.
A Potential New Strategy Against Age-Related Muscle Loss
The discovery could eventually contribute to treatments aimed at maintaining muscle function during aging or extended periods of inactivity.
Muscle deterioration is not limited to older adults. It can also occur during prolonged bed rest or other situations in which muscles are used less frequently. When muscle repair mechanisms become impaired, recovering lost strength and function can become especially challenging.
Rather than replacing the body's natural repair machinery, the approach explored in this study seeks to protect and enhance an existing biological signal. If the benefits can be confirmed in future studies, strengthening HGF activity could become one strategy for supporting muscle regeneration.
The scientists also believe that the underlying effects of LASSS on HGF may extend across species. That raises the possibility of applications not only in human medicine but also in veterinary care, particularly for aging companion animals such as dogs and cats.
For now, the findings represent an early step toward understanding how a naturally occurring muscle repair pathway might be strengthened. Whether LASSS can safely and effectively preserve muscle function during aging remains an open question.
Still, the unexpected discovery that a sulfur-based compound can both protect and enhance a critical repair protein offers a promising direction for future research, with the long-term goal of helping people maintain mobility, independence, and a better quality of life as they grow older.

articles.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
articles.text:
Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.
- Share:
Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a new explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.
Dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.
In a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built new brain circuits around an ancient visual system.
The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.
How the Brain Processes Visual Information
One possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.
Visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.
Some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.
Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.
Because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially important for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.
Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord
The researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).
The first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.
Although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.
The second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.
After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.
This crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.
How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body
The crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three important pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.
The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.
The optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.
Imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.
The movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.
Another important circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.
The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans
The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly important role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.
Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.
All vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.
This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.
The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.
In most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.
In primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.
Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.
The researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely new system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.
A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring
Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.
The researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.
Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.
If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.
The hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.
An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?
The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.
Evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely new systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.
In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.
Under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.
The result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.

articles.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
articles.text:
Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- University of Washington
- Summary:
- A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.
- Share:
Keeping daylight saving time in effect all year could bring brighter evenings, but new research suggests the change would come with a troubling consequence for American children. A nationwide switch could result in at least 2 billion additional trips to school in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks while reducing children's exposure to important morning sunlight.
The debate over permanent daylight saving time has gained momentum in Washington, D.C. This past summer, the U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation that would eliminate the annual return to standard time in the fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already approved measures supporting the change, which would take effect in those states if the federal bill becomes law.
The legislation remains stalled in the Senate, with school start times emerging as a major concern. Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would push sunrise an hour later during the winter months, leaving mornings darker from November through March. Although this would affect everyone traveling early in the day, researchers at the University of Washington wanted to understand what it would mean specifically for children heading to school.
Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Add Billions of Dark School Commutes
To measure the potential impact, the research team examined 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time measures. They combined school enrollment figures, individual school start times, and geographic coordinates to determine how frequently students would need to travel to school before sunrise. The researchers then calculated the total number of these trips under the proposed system and compared it with the current practice of changing clocks twice a year.
The results revealed substantial increases. In Washington state alone, permanent daylight saving time would produce nearly 35 million additional school commutes in darkness. Similar patterns emerged across the other 13 states, with Georgia showing the largest increase at approximately 71 million additional dark trips.
When the researchers extended their findings to estimate the nationwide impact, they calculated that permanent daylight saving time would create at least 2 billion more trips to school before sunrise compared with the current system.
The potential consequences go beyond inconvenient mornings. An analysis of U.S. traffic collision records found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely to occur during dark mornings as after sunrise. The findings were published October 29 in the journal Current Biology.
"It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology at the University of Washington. "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark."
Why Morning Sunlight Matters for Children's Health
Beyond concerns about traffic safety, losing access to morning sunlight could interfere with the body's natural daily rhythms. Bright light early in the day helps synchronize the circadian clock, the internal timing system that influences sleep, mood, appetite, and other important functions. When people receive too little morning light, maintaining these biological rhythms can become more difficult.
For children, who must typically follow fixed school schedules, darker mornings could mean missing a valuable opportunity to receive daylight at a time when their bodies need it.
"When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at the University of Washington. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."
The researchers also identified which communities would experience the greatest changes. Schools located near the western boundaries of time zones, including those in Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected because sunrise already occurs relatively late in those locations. Districts that begin classes early in the morning would face similarly large increases in dark commutes.
Mississippi and Alabama offer striking examples. Schools in both states begin, on average, before 8 a.m. Under the current clock system, each state has approximately 2 million school trips in darkness. With permanent daylight saving time, that figure would rise to more than 20 million trips per state.
"Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."
Why the 2 Billion Estimate May Be Too Low
Although the researchers used detailed school information to calculate changes in 14 states, their nationwide estimate required broader assumptions. To project what would happen if the entire United States adopted permanent daylight saving time, they assumed students would generally be leaving for school at around 8 a.m.
Because many children begin traveling earlier, the team believes the projected increase of approximately 2 billion dark commutes may substantially underestimate the actual impact.
"For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number."
The findings also raise questions about efforts to improve teenagers' sleep by delaying high school start times. Adolescents typically have biological clocks that shift later than those of younger children and adults, making later school schedules beneficial. The researchers argue that permanently moving clocks forward could undermine some of those gains by making morning sunlight less accessible.
One possible solution would be to start school later to compensate for the darker mornings. However, de la Iglesia argues that such a change could have ripple effects throughout daily life, potentially requiring families and workplaces to adjust their schedules as well.
"I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."
The researchers' findings highlight a central tradeoff in the debate over permanent daylight saving time. While eliminating seasonal clock changes would provide more evening sunlight during winter, the additional daylight would come at the expense of morning light, potentially affecting children's safety, sleep, and daily routines.
Additional study authors include high school student Daniel Zhang and University of Washington biology undergraduates Nirekh Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, and Micaela E. Romero.

articles.title: A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials
articles.text:
A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- DOE/Oak Ridge National Laboratory
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a simple mechanical squeeze can dramatically alter the magnetic properties and electrical behavior of exotic materials called altermagnets. The surprising breakthrough could open the door to faster, more energy-efficient electronics and new technologies for quantum computing.
- Share:
Scientists at the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory have discovered that applying a small amount of pressure can dramatically alter the magnetic properties of a promising new class of materials called altermagnets. Using neutron experiments, the researchers uncovered how a simple mechanical squeeze can change the way these materials behave, offering a potential new approach to controlling magnetism.
The results, reported in two consecutive studies published in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, show that mechanical strain can influence both magnetic structures and the movement of electrons. This ability could provide a straightforward way to control materials being investigated for advanced electronic technologies.
Why Altermagnets Matter for Future Electronics
One particularly promising application involves spintronics, short for spin electronics. Unlike conventional electronics, which processes and stores information using the electrical charge of electrons, spintronics also takes advantage of a property known as electron spin.
If scientists can identify and develop suitable materials, including altermagnets, this approach could lead to major advances in technologies ranging from wireless communication to quantum computing.
"By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies," said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.
A Simple Squeeze Reveals Surprising Magnetic Changes
To investigate how pressure affects these materials, the ORNL team placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between a pair of titanium plates and gently compressed them.
Using neutron diffraction at ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source, the scientists examined what happened to the magnetic structures inside the crystals. They found that the applied pressure changed the relative populations of magnetic domains, which are regions within a material that have particular magnetic arrangements. The strain also altered an electrical phenomenon called the anomalous Hall effect, providing evidence that the mechanical squeeze influenced the materials' electrical behavior.
"What's exciting is that one creative experimental idea -- a small mechanical squeeze between two plates -- can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism," said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author on both linked publications.
The findings highlight how a relatively simple experiment can uncover new ways to manipulate magnetic materials, potentially helping researchers develop the building blocks for future spintronic devices.

articles.title: MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
articles.text:
MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
MIT researchers have turned 20 years of materials science thinking upside down, using flexible molecular links to create never-before-seen nanoparticle structures.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy.
- Share:
Scientists have spent decades trying to control how tiny particles connect to form advanced materials. Now, researchers at MIT and their collaborators have discovered that doing the exact opposite of what was previously believed necessary can produce remarkable results.
Instead of relying on rigid molecular connections to hold nanoparticles in carefully planned arrangements, the team developed extremely flexible connectors that bend and adjust as particles come together. This unexpected strategy gives scientists a new way to control how nanoparticles organize themselves, allowing them to create crystal structures that have never been observed before.
The discovery could help overcome a major obstacle in materials science and open new possibilities for creating substances with precisely engineered properties. Potential applications include electronics, medicine, energy technologies, agriculture, and chemical manufacturing.
The findings, described in a paper that will appear in Nature Materials, demonstrate how the flexibility and electrical charges of molecular connectors can determine the structures that nanoparticles form.
MIT Researchers Challenge 20 Years of Materials Science
"People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into," says Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. "This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn't been investigated before. It's exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive. It's the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail. We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well."
The research team also included MIT PhD candidate Nicholas Sbalbi, University of Delaware doctoral student Stephen Kronenberger, MIT undergraduate Hana Shinzawa, Matthew Ye PhD '26, and Arthi Jayaraman, a former professor at the University of Delaware.
At the heart of the discovery is a basic principle of materials science: The way a material's smallest components are arranged determines how that material behaves.
"That means if you know what your building blocks are and how they're arranged, you can explain what properties materials have," Macfarlane says. "Controlling that is how you make materials that have new properties."
This principle is especially important when working with nanoparticles, which are extremely small pieces of matter whose shapes, sizes, and properties can be adjusted for different purposes. Scientists already use individual nanoparticles in technologies involving drug delivery, energy storage, computing, and sensors.
But turning these tiny building blocks into larger, organized materials presents a difficult challenge.
Why Nanoparticles Are So Difficult to Control
One of the biggest obstacles is controlling how nanoparticles attach to one another. Scientists need to determine not only how many neighboring particles each nanoparticle connects with, but also the directions in which those connections form.
Without that control, nanoparticles tend to assemble into tightly packed arrangements that restrict the variety of structures researchers can produce. This limits their ability to create materials with unusual or specialized properties.
Researchers have traditionally approached the problem in two ways. One strategy involves changing the shapes of nanoparticles to influence how they fit together. Another involves modifying specific areas of their surfaces so that only certain regions attract neighboring particles.
In effect, scientists attempt to control where the particles stick to one another, much like designing puzzle pieces that can connect only in particular positions.
Although these methods can produce useful structures, they are often complicated, highly specialized, and difficult to adapt for large-scale production.
"The challenge with both of those approaches is they're difficult to do synthetically as we make the particles," Macfarlane explains. "The methods for defining stickiness that have been developed are always bespoke: They work for one material, at one size scale, in one condition. It's good for studying, but you can't do much with it."
Both strategies also depend on molecular connectors called ligands. These molecules attach to the surfaces of nanoparticles and help link neighboring particles together.
Traditionally, researchers have tried to make these ligands rigid so the connections remain at carefully controlled angles. This helps maintain a desired arrangement, but it also restricts the types of structures that can form and the functions they can perform.
The MIT team decided to explore a radically different possibility.
A Surprising Discovery About Flexible Molecular Bonds
Rather than forcing molecular connectors to remain in fixed positions, the researchers wondered whether giving them almost complete freedom to bend could offer an entirely new form of control.
"We thought, 'Let's do the exact opposite: make the bonds so flexible it doesn't matter what direction they're initially pointing.' The ligands can then reorganize as the particles come together, and that reorganization itself limits how many neighbors each particle can bind," Macfarlane says.
The idea reverses the usual approach to nanoparticle assembly. Instead of controlling the orientation of every connection in advance, the scientists allow the connectors to adjust naturally as the particles interact.
Macfarlane's laboratory has spent years developing ways to construct different types of nanoparticles using attached polymer chains. Polymers are large molecules made of repeating smaller units, and their flexibility makes them useful for creating adjustable molecular connections.
For the new system, the team equipped nanoparticles with highly flexible ligands that carry electrical charges at their ends. Some have positive charges, while others have negative charges.
Because opposite electrical charges attract, the connector molecules naturally bend toward partners with the opposite charge. This attraction helps the nanoparticles join together, while the flexibility of the connectors influences how many connections each particle can make.
"The idea is, instead of defining a specific direction the bonds are going to occur in with complicated synthesis methods, we just said, 'The bonds are going to be as flexible as they want to be, and they'll spontaneously go to whatever valency is going to maximize bond stability,'" Macfarlane says.
In this context, valency refers to the number of connections a nanoparticle forms with its neighbors. By allowing the connectors to move freely, the researchers found that the system could naturally settle into stable arrangements without requiring every connection to be designed beforehand.
Scientists Create Crystal Structures Never Seen Before
Experiments led by Sbalbi demonstrated that the researchers could adjust the connections between nanoparticles by changing two relatively straightforward characteristics: the sizes of the particles and the lengths of their flexible molecular chains.
These adjustments altered how the particles assembled, giving the team control over the number of neighboring particles each one could connect with.
Most importantly, the researchers used this method to produce previously unseen crystal structures.
Crystals are materials whose building blocks form organized, repeating patterns. In this case, the repeating arrangements are made from nanoparticles rather than individual atoms or small molecules. Such ordered nanoparticle networks are often called superlattices.
By reducing the number of connections between neighboring particles, the team was able to create more open arrangements instead of the densely packed structures that commonly form during nanoparticle assembly.
"Without having to predesign where the particles connect or what their shapes are, we can control the number of bonds each particle has," Macfarlane explains. "The amount of flexibility of the polymer dictates how many bonds it has. It allows us to lower the number of bonds each particle has and make lattices we have never seen before."
The results suggest that molecular flexibility, once viewed as an obstacle to precise nanoparticle assembly, can instead become a powerful tool for engineering new material structures.
A New Path Toward Customizable Designer Materials
The researchers believe their method could bring scientists closer to a long-sought goal in materials science: choosing the properties of individual nanoparticles independently of the larger structures into which they assemble.
Ideally, scientists could select nanoparticles for their electrical, optical, chemical, or other useful characteristics and then organize those particles into whatever arrangement best serves a particular application.
In practice, however, existing assembly methods have made that level of flexibility difficult to achieve.
"We in the nanoparticle assembly community talk about having completely independent control over what your particle is and what assembly it goes into," Macfarlane says. "In theory, that should be the case. In reality, it absolutely has not been."
The new approach could help close that gap. Because the researchers can influence nanoparticle arrangements through the flexibility of their connectors and the attraction between electrical charges, they may be able to create a wider variety of structures without the complicated manufacturing techniques required by traditional methods.
The team also sees the discovery as a promising route toward producing customizable materials at larger scales, potentially helping move nanoparticle technologies beyond laboratory experiments and into practical use.
Potential Applications in Electronics, Medicine, and Energy
The ability to build more open and varied nanoparticle structures could prove particularly valuable for developing advanced materials.
In photonics, which involves controlling and manipulating light, precisely organized nanoparticles could help researchers engineer materials with specialized optical properties. In chemical catalysis, where substances accelerate chemical reactions, new particle arrangements could create opportunities to improve the way catalysts operate.
The approach may also support future developments in medicine, agriculture, electronics, and energy technologies.
A major advantage is that nanoparticles can already possess a wide range of desirable properties. By controlling how those particles come together, scientists may be able to combine their individual capabilities in new ways.
"Nanoparticle superlattices offer a way to create designer materials where your building blocks have all sort sorts of unique properties," Macfarlane says. "But just densely packing these nanoparticles together limits your applications. This offers a way to get less dense formations of nanoparticles, and that's where a lot of the interesting applications are."
Although further development will be needed to translate the method into commercial technologies, the discovery establishes molecular flexibility as a new strategy for creating materials with tailored structures.
Instead of treating bending molecular connections as a problem to eliminate, scientists may now be able to use that flexibility to unlock arrangements that rigid designs could not easily achieve.
The research received partial support from the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Army, and the U.S. Navy.

articles.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
articles.text:
NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.
- Share:
NASA is investigating whether private space companies could help extend the life of the Hubble Space Telescope, which has spent more than 35 years transforming our understanding of the universe.
On October 29, the agency issued a Request for Information seeking details about commercial technologies that could be used to service Hubble while it remains in orbit. The goal is to determine whether new spacecraft capabilities could keep the iconic observatory operating longer, improve its performance, or help bring its mission to a safe conclusion.
"Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble's life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe."
NASA Considers Raising Hubble Into a Higher Orbit
One possibility under consideration is sending a spacecraft to push Hubble into a higher orbit. This could counteract the gradual loss of altitude that threatens the telescope's future and potentially allow it to continue making scientific discoveries for additional years.
NASA is also interested in missions that could service the telescope and improve its capabilities. Another option would focus on safely retiring Hubble when its scientific work is complete, either by guiding it through a controlled descent into Earth's atmosphere or arranging for its disposal in orbit.
These possibilities are being explored rather than formally approved. By reaching out to commercial companies, NASA hopes to better understand what technologies are available and whether they could provide practical, affordable solutions.
"Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. "Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble's anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow."
Companies interested in participating can review NASA's Request for Information online. The agency is accepting responses until 3 p.m. EST on Monday, November 30.
Why Hubble Could Fall Back to Earth by 2034
Although Hubble continues to operate in space, its orbit is gradually shrinking. The telescope travels through low Earth orbit, where traces of Earth's atmosphere create drag that slowly reduces the altitude of orbiting spacecraft.
Even hundreds of miles above the planet, the atmosphere is not completely absent. The tiny amount of remaining gas produces resistance as spacecraft move through it. Over long periods, this effect can cause satellites to lose altitude and eventually descend into denser layers of the atmosphere.
Unlike spacecraft equipped with engines that can periodically raise their orbits, Hubble has no propulsion system capable of maintaining its altitude. Without outside assistance, it cannot reverse this gradual orbital decline.
NASA's current analysis suggests that Hubble will likely reenter Earth's atmosphere sometime between 2033 and 2034. To prevent that outcome through an orbital boost, the agency expects that a mission would need to occur by 2032.
That timeline leaves a limited window to evaluate potential solutions, develop a mission, and carry it out before the telescope descends too far.
Extending Hubble's Legacy of Cosmic Discoveries
Since beginning operations more than three decades ago, Hubble has become one of the most influential scientific observatories ever launched. Its observations have helped reshape astronomers' understanding of the cosmos, and the telescope continues to produce discoveries that advance research across many areas of astronomy.
Hubble is also the product of a longstanding international partnership between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency).
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, oversees the telescope and its mission operations, with additional operational support from Denver-based Lockheed Martin Space.
Scientific operations are handled by the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy on NASA's behalf.
With commercial spaceflight technology advancing, NASA is now evaluating whether Hubble could benefit from capabilities that were not available when it was originally designed. A successful mission to raise its orbit or enhance its systems could allow the historic telescope to continue exploring the universe well beyond its currently projected orbital lifetime.

articles.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
articles.text:
SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- SLAC
- Summary:
- For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.
- Share:
For nearly 90 years, physicists have divided magnetic materials into two main categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Now, scientists have confirmed that a third type exists, revealing a previously unrecognized form of magnetic behavior that could lead to major advances in computing and electronics.
The breakthrough comes from a research team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. In a study published in Science, the researchers presented compelling experimental evidence for altermagnetism, a distinct magnetic phase that combines important characteristics of the two traditionally recognized types.
"In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy," explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. "Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase -- altermagnetism -- is real."
The team focused on manganese telluride (MnTe), a material that had long been classified as an antiferromagnet. Building on earlier research, the scientists identified direct evidence of chirality, a distinctive asymmetry in the material's magnetic structure. This property resembles the way a spiral staircase or screw twists in a particular direction and provides a crucial signature of altermagnetism.
Beyond its importance for fundamental physics, the finding could help researchers develop magnetic materials with properties suited to future technologies, including advanced memory systems, quantum devices, and more energy-efficient data centers.
Understanding the Two Traditional Types of Magnetism
Magnetism is familiar from everyday experiences, whether it is a refrigerator magnet holding up a photograph or a compass aligning with Earth's magnetic field. But the physics behind these effects is far more complicated than it appears.
At the atomic level, magnetism is connected to a quantum property of electrons known as spin. Although spin is not literally an electron rotating like a tiny ball, it behaves in certain ways as though the electron has its own angular momentum. Scientists commonly describe the two possible spin orientations as "up" and "down."
When these spins become organized into particular patterns, a material can exhibit magnetic properties. However, that does not necessarily mean it will produce an externally detectable magnetic field.
In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins align in the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down). Their combined effect produces the familiar magnetic field associated with ordinary magnets. People have used materials with this behavior for thousands of years.
A second category, identified in 1933, works differently. In antiferromagnets, neighboring electron spins point in opposite directions (up-down-up-down). Because the magnetic contributions oppose one another, they cancel out, leaving no overall magnetization.
A Third Type of Magnetism Challenges the Old Rules
For almost nine decades, these two categories provided the basic framework for understanding how magnetic order arises in materials. However, experimental observations in recent years began revealing behavior that neither category could fully explain.
Some materials displayed alternating electron spins and no overall magnetization, just like antiferromagnets. Yet they could also support useful spin currents, a property associated with ferromagnetic behavior. Spin currents allow information to be carried through the spin properties of electrons rather than relying entirely on their electrical charge.
The unusual combination suggested that scientists were dealing with something fundamentally different. In 2022, researchers introduced the term "altermagnets" for materials belonging to this proposed third magnetic class.
The key difference lies in the arrangement of atoms within the material. Altermagnets have alternating spin orientations (up-down-up-down), but the crystal structures surrounding the oppositely aligned spins are rotated relative to one another.
This rotation breaks a form of symmetry that exists in conventional antiferromagnets. Although the distinction is subtle, it can dramatically change how electrons behave, allowing altermagnets to combine properties once considered incompatible.
Scientists Find the Missing Evidence for Altermagnetism
Even as experimental support for altermagnetism accumulated, researchers still needed a decisive way to establish that it represented a genuinely distinct magnetic phase.
"By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real," Jost said, "but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle."
That missing evidence involved chirality, a property sometimes described as "handedness." An object is chiral when its mirror image cannot be perfectly aligned with the original. Human hands provide a simple example: Your left and right hands are mirror images, but a left hand cannot fit properly into a right-handed glove.
In an altermagnet, the unusual arrangement of atoms and electron spins can create this kind of handedness in the material's electronic and magnetic structure. Conventional antiferromagnets do not exhibit the same characteristic chiral signature.
Detecting that difference would provide a powerful way to distinguish a true altermagnet from a material that merely resembles one.
The researchers selected manganese telluride as their test material. For decades, scientists considered it an ordinary antiferromagnet, but more recent studies had raised the possibility that it belonged to the newly proposed category.
Powerful X-Rays Reveal a Hidden Magnetic Signature
To investigate the material's unusual properties, the team conducted experiments at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. The facility's ID32 beamline produces precisely controlled polarized X-rays, allowing scientists to examine subtle magnetic structures that are otherwise extremely difficult to detect.
The researchers used circularly polarized X-rays, which have electric fields that rotate in either a left-handed or right-handed direction as the light travels. By measuring how the material scattered these two forms of light, they could search for evidence of chirality.
"Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams," explained Jost. "Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way."
The experiment revealed a clear difference in the way manganese telluride interacted with the two X-ray polarizations. This distinctive chiral response was precisely the kind of signal expected from altermagnetism and would not be present in a conventional antiferromagnet.
"This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own," Jost said.
The researchers first performed the experiment in 2024. They returned in early 2025 and repeated the measurements, successfully reproducing the results and strengthening the evidence for the new magnetic phase.
"This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties," said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. "Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible."
Why Altermagnetism Could Transform Future Computers
The discovery could have important consequences for spintronics, a growing field that seeks to use electron spin to develop more capable electronic devices.
Conventional electronics store and process information primarily by controlling the electrical charge of electrons. Spintronics adds another way to work with information by taking advantage of electron spin as well.
This extra capability could enable devices that operate faster, withstand interference more effectively, and consume substantially less electricity. Such improvements would be especially valuable in computer memory, large data centers, and other technologies that require enormous amounts of information processing.
However, the two traditional types of magnetism present different obstacles that have limited the development of spintronic systems.
"Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields," Jost explained. "If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible -- so you can't easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents."
Altermagnets offer a potentially valuable alternative. Like antiferromagnets, their opposing spins produce no overall magnetization, helping protect them against unwanted magnetic interference. At the same time, their unusual electronic structure allows them to generate spin-polarized currents that can be used to retrieve information.
"Altermagnets combine the best of both," Jost said. "They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with."
A New Frontier for Quantum Technology and Electronics
Confirming altermagnetism gives scientists a new class of materials to investigate and potentially engineer for technological applications. By combining magnetic stability with the ability to manipulate spin-based information, these materials could help overcome challenges that have held back conventional spintronic devices.
The next step will be learning how to control altermagnetic states using external influences such as light and electricity. Researchers hope that mastering this control will make it possible to design practical devices that take advantage of the unusual magnetic properties.
Although significant development is still needed before these materials can be widely used, the findings establish a stronger experimental foundation for future work on quantum technologies, computer memory, and more efficient data centers.
The research received partial funding from the DOE Office of Science.
