articles.title: Canva lays off over 1,200 people amid slowing growth | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Design software maker Canva is cutting 22% of its staff, amounting to 1,271 people, amid a growth slowdown.
The company’s co-founder and CEO, Melanie Perkins, in a note to employees said while Canva has scaled so far, it needs to change to address slowing growth.
“Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination, and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade,” Perkins wrote.
Canva is reshuffling its organizational chart and merging its product, growth, and platform teams to reduce communication friction. The company is also reducing “subspecialisation,” which means its employees might be asked to take up more responsibilities. The company is also moving toward hybrid work and asking people to work from an office a few days a week.
The company has been shipping its own AI models to reduce costs and reliance on third-party models, but it still had to cut its revenue growth forecast to 20% from 30% to address ballooning AI costs. This also resulted in Canva’s early investors cutting its valuation to about $35 billion earlier this year.
Canva is also facing increasing competition from AI startups and general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, whose image generation capabilities allow people to easily put together posters and presentations.

articles.title: Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month
articles.text:
Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced plans for “AI-native” devices and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it won’t have is a screen:
Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month
CEO Carl Pei says Nothing’s first ‘AI-native’ device ‘couldn’t have been an app.’
“Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. Last month, a rumor claimed Nothing is planning to launch two pairs of AI smart glasses, including one without cameras, and an earlier rumor said it’s “repositioning itself as an AI-first company” with a shift to AI accessories.
Nothing’s AI device wouldn’t be the first screen-free AI gadget, following the likes of the Humane AI pin, the Friend, and even AI stuffed animals. OpenAI is also reportedly working on an AI smart speaker with Jony Ive. Pei alluded to earlier AI devices, saying, “the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life.” He added, “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end.”

articles.title: Apple will check shared iCloud links for ‘harmful content’
articles.text:
Apple will start checking iCloud items that are accessible to anyone who has the link for “harmful content” starting with iOS 27.3 and other 27.3 updates, the company says.
Apple will check shared iCloud links for ‘harmful content’
If you make an item on iCloud available to anyone who has the link, Apple will be able to check it starting with iOS 27.3.
“When you share an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, that content is made accessible to Apple to check for harmful content,” according to a support document reported on by 9to5Mac. Sharing something over iCloud with the “Anyone with the Link” permissions will also mean that it’s no longer end-to-end encrypted.
Apple’s support document does not define what “harmful content” is. But this new approach follows calls from protestors for Apple to crack down on child sexual abuse material stored in iCloud.
Apple says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” any harmful content that a user attempts to upload. Apple may also block or disable accounts, prevent a user from making a new account, or, “if necessary,” invoke law enforcement.
The company launched the first 27.3 developer betas yesterday, and said recently it plans to launch iOS 27.3 in December.

articles.title: NextDC shares surge 43% after Goodman, Digital Realty stake purchases
articles.text:
Shares of Australian data center operator NextDC surged more than 42% Thursday after Goodman Group and U.S.-listed data center operator Digital Realty moved to acquire stakes of up to 9.9% in the company.
In a regulatory filing on the same day, NextDC said the two companies conducted an aftermarket bookbuild Wednesday, seeking shares at A$9.50 apiece.
NextDC's board called the move "opportunistic," noting that it came two weeks after the company disclosed a power supply delay at its M3 Melbourne data center and revised its fiscal 2027 guidance.
The company said it was not aware of the outcome of the share purchase. Goodman and Digital Realty told investors they had no current intention of making a takeover bid, but reserved the right to do so.
NextDC's rally came against a backdrop of weakness in U.S. data center stocks overnight. Shares of CoreWeave fell about 9%, while Iren dropped roughly 11.2% on Wednesday.
The sell-off followed sweeping Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections, which raised expectations of tighter scrutiny and potential restrictions on data center development that could slow the AI infrastructure buildout.

articles.title: Inside India newsletter: India weighs a tax cut to win over foreign investors. Will it work?
articles.text:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.
Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.
Once a favorite emerging market for foreign investors, Indian equities have been losing their charm. Foreign holdings of Indian stocks are currently at an all-time low of 14%. Now a tax cut, which puts India on par with several Asian markets, is being proposed to win back these investors.
This week, I spoke with experts to find out whether a tax cut alone can restore the Indian stock market's appeal to foreign investors.
Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.
The big story
The clamor for removing tax on long-term capital gains, or LTCG, on foreign portfolio investors is rising in India as the country's equity markets witness record capital outflows.
On Monday, Reuters reported that India's capital market regulator has urged the government to scrap the LTCG tax for foreign investors.
One of India's oldest and most prominent industry bodies, PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, last week asked the government appealing to abolish the tax.
It argued that the capital gains tax was increased in 2024 at a time when the stock market was "near record highs" and as the market conditions have now changed, the government needs to review it.
The country's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday acknowledged the exit of foreign capital outflows and added she would consider the calls for reviewing LTCG tax, as per local media reports.
These demands come at a time when foreign investors' appetite for Indian equities has sharply declined. As per a Nomura report on Monday, foreign holdings in Indian stocks are at an all-time low of 14%.
Experts agree that the removal of the tax cut would improve foreign investors' sentiment by putting India's tax regime on par with other emerging markets. But the tax cut alone may not be enough to bring back foreign investors in droves, they said.
"A tax cut helps at the margin, but allocators tend to buy expected returns, not tax breaks," said Amit Bhartia, portfolio manager at Singapore-based Delorean Partners. He added that foreign investors have exited India as earnings growth became less predictable, while risks shot up.
Bhartia highlighted that foreign investors put in about 570 billion rupees ($6 billion) into Indian equities in September of 2024, and a month later pulled out 940 billion rupees to chase cheaper Chinese stocks. "The tax rate didn't change between those two months. The perceived relative return did," Bhartia explained.
Until the record exit in March this year, the outflows in October 2024 were the highest in a month.
Rising risks
Multiple risks are weighing down Indian markets right now, including strained ties with the U.S., higher energy prices, a depreciating currency and uncertainty over the impact of artificial intelligence.
A possible LTCG cut for foreign investors, a drop in global bond yields and expectations of the rupee holding up on central bank intervention would lend support to the Indian markets, Nomura said in its report.
However, it added that from a longer-term perspective, concerns around geopolitical and technological uncertainty persist, "weighing on long-term growth expectations."
India was the world's third worst-performing market after Indonesia and Turkey between January and October this year, the report showed. India's benchmark Nifty 50 as lost nearly 9% so far this year.
Foreign investors, who just three years ago celebrated India as the best-performing emerging market, have soured over the last two years, cashing out net $18.9 billion in 2025 and more than $30 billion so far this year.
India has "to fight for capital in a competition it could once afford to take for granted," global brokerage Bernstein said in a report on Monday. It argued that multiple "catalysts," including a tax cut and easing of tensions in the Middle East, are needed to reverse capital outflows from India.
"India's valuations remain expensive, while earnings growth has been disappointing," the report said.
As per the data shared in the report, India is trading at a rolling 12-month forward price-to-earnings of 18.6 times, higher than Taiwan's 16.8 times and Korea's 3.9 times. Both these markets have been outperformers in the emerging countries, propped up by strong artificial intelligence names.
On the earnings growth front, while emerging markets on average are expected to deliver a 45% improvement, India's forecast is much slower at 11%, as per Bernstein.
The tax cut alone will not "trigger a major reallocation into Indian equities as the fundamental trade-off facing foreign investors remains unchanged," Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC.
As cracks emerge in the global AI rally, data from LSEG shows Indian benchmark indexes have outperformed global peers over the past month, as some investors see the Indian market as a hedge against AI. Foreign capital flows at the start of this month have been positive. But will they sustain?
India has a strong structural growth story, but investors still need earnings growth to justify the valuation premium, Luchnikava-Schorsch said.

Canadian firm Fairfax Financial Holdings' proposed $5.5 billion takeover of IDBI Bank is facing pushback from employees of the Indian state-owned lender and political parties in the country.

articles.title: White House panel delays hearing on Fed's Lisa Cook to Dec. 14
articles.text:
A White House committee of inquiry postponed from Thursday to Dec. 14 a hearing with Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook for an investigation of whether allegations of false statements in mortgage applications warrant her firing by President Donald Trump, a White House official said Wednesday evening.
But it was unclear if Cook, whom Trump unsuccessfully tried to fire in August 2025, would agree to attend.
The official said the postponement came at the request of Cook.
Her lawyer Abbe Lowell last month said questions about the committee's fairness and objectivity would have to be addressed before the hearing could occur.
Lowell also said the hearing could not take place until December, at the earliest, because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."
The New York Times first reported the hearing's rescheduling.
Trump in early October established the committee to investigate allegations that Cook made false statements related to "one or more mortgage instruments."
"The Committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook's removal within the meaning of" a federal law that was cited in a Supreme Court ruling in June that temporarily blocked her firing.
The committee is comprised of Kevin Hassett, assistant to the president for economic policy, Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and Office of Government Ethics Director Keith Sonderling.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing.
In a lawsuit challenging her firing, she argued that Trump's claim about the mortgage statements is pretextual, and that his real reason for trying to oust her is her refusal to agree to his demands that she vote for lower interest rates.
Trump created the panel more than three months after the Supreme Court ruled that the president, for now, could not fire Cook from the central bank's board.
The ruling kept in place a lower court's order preventing Cook from being terminated while the suit challenging her dismissal proceeds.
The decision did not determine whether Trump ultimately has the power to fire a Fed board member. But it said she could remain on the board as her suit was pending because she was not given due process to challenge her firing.
The committee of inquiry Trump set up may be designed to show the Supreme Court that Cook has now received due process.
CNBC has requested comment from Lowell.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says this fast food giant has more room to run
articles.text:
McDonald's turnaround efforts are beginning to pay off and investors will likely be rewarded with more upside ahead, CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday.
The fast-food giant's third-quarter earnings showed signs of progress in its struggling domestic business. U.S. same-store sales declined 0.2%, better than the 0.5% drop Wall Street expected, and returned to growth in September after falling in July and August. Encouraging traffic trends continued into October.
McDonald's shares surged 6.5% Wednesday, extending the rebound from their early-October lows to more than 20%. At the low, the stock had lost roughly a third of its value from its all-time high in March amid weakening U.S. sales and growing competition from a revitalized Burger King.
"We're seeing progress for the Golden Arches, and that's why the stock is doing so much better than it was just a couple of months ago," the "Mad Money" host said. "I still like McDonald's – I'm glad I stuck with it, and I think you're going to get higher prices for this stock."
Cramer on Oct. 1 described McDonald's as a "show me" story after a disappointing September investor day raised concerns about the cost of restaurant renovations and franchisee support for the plan. Nevertheless, he called the stock "tempting," and said he'd rather be a buyer at those levels than a seller.
McDonald's intensified its focus on affordability during the September quarter, restoring digital promotions and shifting marketing toward value offerings, including $5 and $6 meal deals. "The interventions we made in the U.S. began to stabilize baseline guest counts, and we saw progress through the quarter," CEO Chris Kempczinski told Cramer on Wednesday morning.
Still, the quarter wasn't perfect and challenges remain. McDonald's missed revenue expectations, while weakness in France weighed on international results. McDonald's plans to expand entry-level value offerings, strengthen digital promotions and improve food quality and service. The company is also testing two new value menus, with plans to roll out the stronger option nationwide in early 2027.
With shares well above their October lows, Cramer cautioned that further gains will depend on sustained execution rather than an attractive valuation alone.
"McDonald's shares were extremely compelling on a valuation basis at their lows a month ago – that's why I had confidence sticking with the stock even when the fundamentals looked weak," he said. "With the stock well off its lows at this point, we'll need to see continued execution for McDonald's shares to continue their run back towards the highs set earlier this year."

articles.title: A 'demand decade' ahead for energy? BP, Baker Hughes CEOs weigh the investment outlook
articles.text:
Rising energy demand is creating new investment opportunities even as geopolitical risks and uncertain oil prices challenge the industry.
Baker Hughes CEO Lorenzo Simonelli is optimistic about the longer-term outlook, pointing to AI, population growth and developing nations as factors supporting continued energy demand growth.
"I think we have a 'demand decade' ahead of us," Simonelli told CNBC's Dan Murphy on "Access Middle East" at the ADIPEC energy conference in Abu Dhabi. "We're looking at very much seeing capital investments improve and increase over time," as growing consumption will require additional infrastructure to support demand.
However, turning that demand into profitability may be a challenge.
Markus Krebber, CEO of German energy company RWE, said AI and electrification were driving electricity demand, but geopolitical tensions, supply chain pressures and higher interest rates were complicating investment decisions.
"You have huge investment opportunity, but on the other hand, a very challenging investment environment," Krebber said during a separate ADIPEC discussion. On planned expansions in computing capacity and the power needed to support them, he said "it's going to come, but it probably comes slow."
The wide range of global energy demand forecasts is an important consideration in investment decisions, given that new oil and gas projects can take years to develop and remain in production for decades, BP CEO Meg O'Neill said at ADIPEC.
She also highlighted the uncertainty surrounding oil prices, saying that "we need to plan our business for a lower-price environment."
Industry activity
Industry activity is expected to rise by a low-single-digit percentage in 2027, according to Simonelli. The Middle East conflict has highlighted the need for more resilient energy infrastructure, including additional storage and pipelines, he said.
"If you look at the energy system, though, what it really means is it's going to have to be more resilient," Simonelli said. "That means more storage. It means more pipelines. It means eliminating choke points that exist today."
Schneider Electric CEO Olivier Blum noted that some projects in the Persian Gulf have slowed because of the Middle East conflict. However, "in the mid-term, I would say the opportunity for more infrastructure has even increased," he told CNBC.
The investment equation also depends on the supply outlook, of course.
Oil markets could face oversupply in 2027 and 2028, Richard Bronze, co-founder and head of geopolitics at energy consultancy Energy Aspects, told CNBC in a separate interview.
Supply-demand forecasts, including those from Energy Aspects, "project an oversupplied market 2027, 2028 — if we get Middle Eastern flows back to normal," Bronze said.

articles.title: Jim Cramer warns investors may be reading too much into Wall Street's post-election rally
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer warned Wednesday that Wall Street may be getting ahead of itself following the midterm elections.
Stocks rallied after Democrats scored a decisive victory in the midterms, but the gains masked a divide within technology. Hyperscalers surged as investors anticipated that greater opposition to data center development could slow the AI buildout and ease spending pressures. Meanwhile, semiconductor stocks and data center developers came under pressure. Cramer cautioned that investors may be drawing premature conclusions about the election's economic implications.
"The midterm results controlled today's trading, but by Friday we will be talking the Labor Department's nonfarm payrolls report, and we could see a repeal of so much of this move that I hesitate to guess where we go next," the "Mad Money" host said.
"But I do like the word guess," he added. "Because that sums up what I saw throughout today's session and it's not the stuff I want to base investment decisions on, even as it's terrific for a one-day trade for the ages."
Apple shares hit an all-time high Wednesday as investors bet that a slowdown in data center construction could ease memory chip prices, which have been pressuring the company's margins. Microsoft and Amazon also rallied on expectations that a slower AI buildout could reduce data center costs and rein in their massive capital spending.
Conversely, investors sold shares of companies whose growth depends on continued AI infrastructure investment, including chipmakers Nvidia and AMD and data center developers CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren.
But Cramer questioned whether a single election could fundamentally alter the forces driving the market. "I want you to understand that, as important as a midterm election can be, and this one is important, the elections did not upend the business cycle," Cramer said.
Cramer noted that he's aligned with JPMorgan strategist Michael Cembalest, who publishes the closely followed Eye on the Market commentary.
In his latest piece Wednesday, Cembalest wrote, "The business cycle drives markets, and the important components are things that midterms do not affect: 10 yr interest rates, commodity prices, Fed policy, corporate profits, budget deficits, defense spending, the pace of AI investment over the next 12 months, the ferocious borrowing needs of AI companies and the impact on credit spreads, etc."
Cramer said it's important that investors understand that short-term market moves may not always align with the actual fundamentals. "Never confuse what happens in the stock market with what happens in reality," he said.
Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of AAPL, AMZN, MSFT, and NVDA.

articles.title: What Wall Street billionaires are saying about Democrats' midterm sweep
articles.text:
America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.
As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory, some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending. Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock, reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.
"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn, calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the threshold reporting in the 2026 election cycle.
His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor, watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.
Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, another major political donor, took a sharper tone.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X, accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.
Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.
But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep: the future of the AI boom.
Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.
Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.
"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election-night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.
Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data-center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data-center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.
AMD CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion, urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC Wednesday.
Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.
Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday, adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data-center operators tumbled.

articles.title: Stock futures are little changed after big rally following Democrats' decisive midterm wins
articles.text:
U.S. equity futures rose on Wednesday evening following a rally on the heels of a sharp decline in the price of oil and certainty around the Democrats' midterm wins.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 90 points, or 0.2%. S&P 500 futures were up 0.1%, and Nasdaq-100 futures were flat.
After the bell on Wednesday, chipmaker Qualcomm reported earnings that beat estimates, but fell 6.5%. AppLovin, the artificial intelligence-powered advertising company, surged almost 24% after delivering better-than-expected results and issuing guidance that beat estimates.
Stocks on Wednesday rallied as oil prices dipped, with West Texas Intermediate crude futures falling more than 8% to settle at $88.12 a barrel. The Dow gained more than 1,500 points, or 3%, to post its best day since April 2025, while the S&P 500 advanced 1.6%.
Those moves came after Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for Republican losses in the midterms on Tuesday.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 0.49% on Thursday, while the Topix rose over 2%. South Korea's Kospi was down 2.33%, and the tech-focused, small-cap Kosdaq fell 1.24%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 1.39%.
Trading on Wednesday stateside showed investors adjusting to midterm results, which showed Democrats flipping control of the House of Representatives and Senate — securing comfortable majorities in both chambers — and a slew of governorships, too.
Consumer discretionary names such as Walmart helped lead the way higher on Wednesday, with the retail giant up more than 3% in the regular session. At the same time, names linked to the data center build-out, like CoreWeave, fell on worries about a backlash to the industry in light of election results in various states. In Texas, for instance, Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the election for governor after calling for tougher restrictions on data center development.
But Jordan Watson, a portfolio manager at Tandem Investment Advisors, said the big rally and the rotation away from artificial intelligence names could be temporary.
"We may be headed for more volatility as investors digest the election results and potential policy implications," he said. "I wouldn't view [Wednesday's equity trading] as an all-clear signal, but rather a call for some sanity around the amount of capital being poured into the AI infrastructure build-out and whether those investments will generate the returns investors expect."
Going into Thursday, traders will be watching for weekly jobless claims data. October's nonfarm payrolls report is due on Friday.
On the earnings front, Tapestry, Kimberly-Clark and ConocoPhillips are expected to report in the morning, followed by Airbnb and Akamai in the afternoon.

articles.title: Democrats flip dozens of GOP seats. Republicans haven't flipped a single one
articles.text:
Seven Senate seats. At least 24 House districts. Five governorships. Twelve state legislative chambers. By Wednesday afternoon, that's how far Democrats' historic midterm rout had reached.
Republicans, meanwhile, had yet to flip a single Democratic-held congressional seat, governorship or state legislative chamber, according to Associated Press data. Their remaining opportunities for congressional pickups are largely confined to two newly gerrymandered House districts that weren't even supposed to be competitive in the first place.
The lopsided results underscored the breadth of the GOP's shellacking, with Democrats breaking decades of Republican dominance in reliably red states and reshaping the balance of power from Washington to state capitols.
As of late Wednesday, nine House seats remained uncalled by the AP along with two Senate seats and two governors races. The one seat Republicans may have a chance of flipping that hasn't been redistricted ahead of this election is Maine's 2nd District, FiftyPlusOne head of research Mary Radcliffe said by email.
In Kansas, voters elected their first Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, ending a 94-year losing streak for the party. In Texas, Democrats toppled three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and captured a Senate seat that had eluded the party since 1988. Republican-held Senate seats also fell in Iowa, South Carolina and Ohio, along with seats in Maine and North Carolina.
The same wave swept through governors' mansions. Democrats scored upsets in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Nevada — all states President Donald Trump won in 2024 — giving the party a majority of the nation's governorships for the first time since 2010.
Upheaval even reached state capitols, where Republican legislative majorities that had endured for decades fell like dominoes.
Democrats seized control of the Texas House for the first time in more than two decades, flipped both chambers of the Wisconsin Legislature and wrested the North Carolina House from Republicans after 16 years in the minority.
In Pennsylvania, Democrats captured the state Senate for the first time since before 1994, giving the party complete control of state government. They also reclaimed lower chambers in Michigan and Minnesota, restoring full Democratic control in both states. In Arizona, unofficial results pointed toward Democrats taking both legislative chambers for the first time in roughly 60 years.
Even where Republicans held on to legislative majorities, Democrats stripped away veto-proof supermajorities in Florida, Indiana, Kansas and Missouri. Not since the aftermath of Watergate in 1974 had the GOP faced a statehouse reckoning of this magnitude, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.
The scale of the losses is all the more remarkable given how aggressively Republicans had tried to protect their power. At Trump's urging, GOP lawmakers spent months pursuing an extraordinary mid-decade redistricting campaign, redrawing congressional boundaries in Texas, Florida and North Carolina to tilt the electoral map in their favor.
Yet the gerrymandering push did little to blunt the Democratic wave. And the damage might not be over. Republicans were still fighting to hold Senate seats in Alaska and Mississippi, with several House contests also yet to be called Wednesday.
— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

articles.title: Cramer: What must happen for Home Depot to keep its 25% monthlong rally going
articles.text: Home Depot was one of our biggest post-election winners. Wednesday's 6.5% gain extended a recent hot streak and flipped the struggling stock positive year to date. The question now for patient Home Depot investors like us is whether this is the turning point we've been waiting for, or just another head fake. Home Depot and other housing stocks rallied on the hope that the Democratic sweep on Capitol Hill in Tuesday's midterms could lead to an easing of America's affordability crisis and a pick-up in the stagnant housing market. Oil prices, which have driven rekindled inflation this year, tumbled on hopes that the Middle East conflict may not worsen. Bond yields, which are sensitive to inflation expectations, also fell. "If rates come down or [the] do-it-yourself market heats up, you're going to have the number one stock," Jim said during Wednesday, referring to Home Depot. "We have the number one stock." The bounce in Home Depot goes beyond Wednesday, which was also a stellar session for the overall market. It's going to take more than a day to see whether Wall Street truly embraces what will become the Democratic majority in both the House and Senate. What we do know, however, is that Home Depot has been quietly rallying for a month. Since the 10-year Treasury yield hit a two-decade high above 5.3% on Oct. 5, the Club stock is up more than 25%. In fact, it is on pace for five straight positive weeks, which would mark its longest weekly win streak since November 2024 into the first week of December 2024. Tracking the 10-year is important because mortgage rates tend to follow the long end of the bond market yield curve. According to the Mortgage Bankers Association , the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.5% the week of Oct. 14 — a level not seen since November 2023. While rates have come down a couple of weeks in a row, they are still a full percentage point higher than a year ago. That has kept a lid on housing activity, which has held Home Depot back on both renovations and new construction. To be sure, management has been controlling what it can control — getting bigger with acquisitions to better serve the Pro customer, while matching and topping rival Lowe's in same-store sales growth. HD mountain 2024-11-04 Home Depot 2-year peformance Unfortunately, we have been here before in recent years — signals that mortgage rates might start cooperating and Home Depot stock rallying off recent lows. Jim believes the election outcome could pave the way for relief on tariffs, another major headwind on Home Depot stock. "The working person's been hurt by higher gasoline. The working person's been hurt by tariffs, including many things that are bought at Home Depot," he said. "That's going to be over." articles.title: Prediction markets cement their status after forecasting Democratic sweep of Congress
articles.text:
Prediction market platforms cemented their role in election forecasting on Tuesday, when markets accurately predicted a host of races before the polls closed, and projected outcomes before news outlets.
Democrats were seen as favored to flip both the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate on prediction markets before the first polls closed at 6:00 p.m. ET Tuesday, and were seen as narrow favorites to take at least 53 Senate seats, while a 54th was forecast as a toss-up.
So far, Democrats have won 54 Senate seats — including wins in Iowa, which prediction markets placed at 50-50 odds, and South Carolina, where Republicans narrowly favored. Outstanding results remain in Mississippi and Alaska, where prediction markets give Democrat Scott Colom and Mary Peltola 90% odds of winning.
Leading prediction market platforms were actively projecting races on X Tuesday night. Those projections, at times, came before many media outlets made their own projections, or before even a substantial number of votes had been counted.
Confident calls
Kalshi was confident making those calls, as long as odds for a candidate were above 99% and trading activity for the opposite candidate "dried out," said Jack Such, a spokesperson for the platform.
Polymarket celebrated on X how it projected races, saying that in 10 key races, the platform called races ahead of outlets including CNN, Fox News and the Associated Press by a median 31 minutes.
"It's now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks," said Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan in an X post. "No knock to them, but now there's Polymarket, and many people are realizing they want to know what's happening in real time."
Even in races where markets initially favored the candidate who eventually lost, they quickly adjusted once initial vote counts came in. In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews was seen as the favorite on Kalshi to win shortly after 7:30 p.m., only 30 minutes after polls closed. In Texas, where Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, Hinojosa's odds on Polymarket jumped from 39% to 73% within five minutes of initial poll closings.
"You now have financially motivated number crunchers doing this, around the world, that give you that signal just that much faster," said Flip Pidot, a member of the board of directors at the Coalition for Political Forecasting.
Still, a successful night for prediction markets shouldn't stop efforts aimed at stronger regulation of the platforms, said Michelle Kendler-Kretsch, a researcher at the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, a nonprofit. She cited a recent Reuters/Ipsos survey that found most Americans are against using prediction markets to trade on elections.
"Risks and vulnerabilities didn't change overnight just because the markets were accurate this time around," she said.
Before the midterms
Right before the midterms, prediction market forecasts had missed major global elections, including Brazil's presidential race, where Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva only had about 20% odds to win on Kalshi before polls closed.
Prediction markets also whiffed in some high-profile Democratic primaries over the summer, forecasting extremely high odds for progressives in Wisconsin and Michigan, for example. The Michigan Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed, narrowly won his primary before going on to win Thursday's general election.
Academics who've researched prediction markets for decades say the platforms aren't wrong when candidates with low odds on markets end up winning races.
"If you toss two coins, there's a 25% chance that you'll throw two heads in a row, and nobody would be terribly surprised if you did," said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College.
Despite their early success on Tuesday, Dartmouth College economic professor Eric Zitzewitz said it's still not clear if casual observers understand how market probabilities work.
"Some people who are coming to [prediction markets] for the first time will see 55 by 45 odds and think that, 'Oh the candidate with 55 is way ahead,'" he said.
As prediction markets gain traction, however, the public will improve at understanding how to interpret their odds, Zitzewitz said.
With another election under their belts, prediction markets will remain a force through the next presidential election, experts said.
"Last time around [in 2024], prediction markets were in the discussion, but they were in the discussion in a way that was a little bit unsure," said Harry Crane, a professor of statistics at Rutgers University. "This [was] the first true prediction markets election."
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title: Figma sinks after earnings beat as company prioritizes long-term growth with AI changes
articles.text:
Figma shares tumbled 7% in extended trading after the company reported third-quarter results and guidance that surpassed Wall Street's predictions.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings per share: 10 cents adjusted vs. 5 cents expected
- Revenue: $391.4 million vs. $375.8 million expected
Figma's revenue grew about 43% year over year in the quarter, according to a statement. Net loss narrowed to $81.3 million, or 15 cents per share, compared with a loss of $1.10 billion, or $2.72 per share, a year earlier.
The company's 12% adjusted operating margin exceeded the 6.1% consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount.
Executives lifted the full-year forecast. Figma now anticipates an 11% operating margin, up from 9% as of August, and $1.497 billion to $1.499 billion in revenue, compared with $1.463 billion to $1.467 billion before. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.471 billion in 2026 revenue.
The company sees fourth-quarter revenue growth slowing to about 33%. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted 28% growth.
Figma's announcement comes a day after highly valued design software startup Canva said it would cut 22% of its employees.
Shares have come down about 41% so far in 2026, while the S&P 500 index has gained 12%. Earlier this year, investors became concerned that artificial intelligence models could pose a competitive risk to Figma. Across much of software, AI panic has largely subsided as incumbents have posted persistent growth.
Figma wants to benefit from the rising adoption of AI to build websites and apps. During the quarter, the company started giving more AI credits to clients while maintaining prices.
"What that means is you're potentially trading off near-term revenue, investing in your customers, and then allowing yourself to then grow durably over the long term," Figma's finance chief, Praveer Melwani, told CNBC in an interview on Wednesday.
The number of weekly users working at organizations that spend over $10,000 on Figma who used AI credits increased by almost 50% during the quarter, Figma said in the statement. The share of work the company's own AI model performs doubled, and the rate of people undoing AI-generated work has fallen.
"If there's certain actions that we can power for our customers at lower latency, lower cost, or similar quality to third party, we're open to that as well," Melwani said.
Figma is increasing its focus on cybersecurity, said Dylan Field, Figma's co-founder and CEO. In recent months, AI agents have infiltrated systems at Hugging Face and other companies.
Clients aren't asking Figma to become a security vendor, but the company must scrutinize "the security of all of our vendors right now," Field said.

articles.title: What was really behind Wednesday's monster rally? Trump quickly making peace
articles.text:
The stock market skyrocketed on Wednesday on the heels of a decisive sweep for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections. But that was not necessarily the only driver of the climb.
"President Trump's acknowledgement of the Democrats' victory in the midterms and his expressed openness to collaborating with the opposition have helped markets to rally on hopes that contestation of the results and more adverse polarization can be avoided," said Thomas Hempell, Generali Investments senior economist.
Trump told The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal overnight Tuesday that he accepted the results and would work with Democrats. Those headlines coincided with a rebound in stock market futures.
In the lead-up to this year's midterms, some on Wall Street grew increasingly concerned about the prospect of Trump contesting the election results. The Department of Justice's Alaska election lawsuit led to fears over delays with the outcome that would exacerbate the uneasiness in the market that's typically removed once the elections conclude.
CNBC's Fed Survey showed that among 30 fund managers, strategists and economists, 63% believe that the extended uncertainty around the balance of power created by legal challenges to the election results posed "some" market risk. That was a slight increase from 61% in September. Additionally, 14% believed it represented "significant" market risk, which was up from 7%.
Now, investors are breathing a sigh of relief over Trump's acceptance of the results, which should "act as a break on extreme policy outcomes and bring down risk premia," so long as the president's decision remains, said George Saravelos, head of FX Research at Deutsche Bank.
'An X factor'
Trump has a history of rallying markets, as well as driving them lower, with his announcements. Jay Woods of Freedom Capital Markets, who noted that the rebound in stocks overnight was partially due to the president's "initial tone and reaction to the results," said the focus will shift to whether Trump's latest move will actually have staying power.
"I think Trump is going to try to do and say the right thing, but at two in the morning, he may change his mind," the chief market strategist said. "He is an X factor."
Woods added that he's "encouraged" by Wednesday's massive rally, but he noted that there are still headwinds that could plague the market over the coming weeks — such as concerns about inflationary pressures as a result of higher energy prices from the conflict in the Middle East.
"How Trump reacts to it will help us navigate those headwinds," he said.
Osaic's Philip Blancato said he believes that if Trump "continues to play nice" with Democrats, the market is going to have a "very strong" end to the year.
Stocks historically tend to rally after the midterms anyway, but this time around, some were worried the solid run-up in the S&P 500 this year was going to potentially hinder those gains. After Trump's reaction, Blancato said he doesn't think the S&P 500 hitting 8,000 by year-end is totally out of the question and that there's "a lot predicated on him, but not completely."
The broad market index gained more than 1% on Wednesday, with its closing price implying a roughly 4% gain to that level.
However, investors should be prepared for any future volatility if Trump's rhetoric does not remain the same, the chief market strategist said.
"The president's always going to be a wildcard," he said. "Let's not let one day make a year. This is an instant reaction to this thing. There's still plenty of things to be hashed out."

articles.title: Snap shares fall over 10% on third-quarter revenue miss
articles.text:
Snap shares sank over 10% when the Snapchat parent missed on revenue and daily active users in its third-quarter earnings report Wednesday.
Here's how the company did compared with analysts' expectations:
- Earnings per share: $0.19 adj. vs. $0.16 expected, according to LSEG
- Revenue: $1.72 billion vs. $1.73 billion expected, according to LSEG
- Global daily active users: 495 million vs. 499 million expected, according to StreetAccount
- Global average revenue per user, or ARPU: $3.48 vs. $3.48 expected, according to StreetAccount
Sales in Snap's third quarter jumped 14% year-over-year while net income came in at $56 million, compared to the $104 million net loss it logged the prior year.
Snap's third-quarter adjusted earnings came in at $383 million, topping the $337 million that analysts were projecting, according to StreetAccount.
The Snapchat parent said fourth-quarter revenue should come in between $1.95 billion and $1.99 billion. The midpoint of that figure is higher than Wall Street's estimates of $1.95 billion.
Fourth-quarter adjusted earnings are expected to come in between $490 million and $525 million. Analysts were expecting that figure to be $498 million.
Snap executives said in an investor letter that the company plans for globally monthly active users to become its "primary audience metric" starting in its first quarter for 2027. The company also said it has 977 MAU for the quarter.
"Daily engagement has historically been stable as a percentage of monthly engagement, but we do not intend to optimize Snapchat around daily use at the expense of long-term value for our community," the investor letter said. "A longer-term horizon better aligns our reported metrics with the product and safety decisions that strengthen relationships, create lasting utility, and support broader, more durable audience growth."
Snap chief commercial officer Ronan Harris told analysts during an earnings call that lower spending by unspecified consumer packaged goods, or CPG, companies impacted third-quarter sales. Harris attributed the curbed CPG spending to "macro pressures in the U.S. and also the Middle East."
"As we look ahead, we're seeing very positive signs of growth from diversified verticals like financial services in the U.S.," Harris said. "So part of our strategy here is to look outside of the pressures in CPG and find traction in these other verticals."
WATCH: Jim Cramer talks the capex spending outlook for 2027.

articles.title: The economy brought Trump back to power. Now it's his downfall
articles.text:
As President Donald Trump campaigned for the nation's highest office in 2024, he regularly blamed Democrats for the country's economic anxiety.
During campaign stops across the U.S., Trump frequently asked voters if they were better off than they were four years prior. At the time, his message appeared to land: In an election centered on inflation and the cost of living, Trump won every swing state and the nationwide popular vote.
Two years later, voters grappling with those same kitchen-table issues took away much of his party's power in Washington and in states across the country.
Democrats rode a blue wave of historic proportions in Tuesday's midterm election to flip everything from battleground congressional seats to long-held Republican governorships. The Democratic Party will now have control of both the House and Senate, ending the Republican Party's trifecta of power in the federal government.
Nearly nine out of 10 voters in the CNBC Voter Poll said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Participants in the poll ranked the economy as the most important issue facing the country during the midterm election, ahead of topics like the state of democracy and immigration. Three out of every four survey participants rated the economy as "poor" or "not so good," compared with just 2% who described it as "excellent."
And perhaps most telling of all: Fewer than one out of every five voters said their family's financial standing was better than it was two years ago.
Much of their dissatisfaction was centered on Trump himself, with about two out of every three voters saying his policies worsened economic conditions in the country.
"It was all about the economy," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Most Americans are struggling with the high inflation and have been for quite some time, and they're just angry."
A 'breaking point'
Tuesday's election played out against the backdrop of a war with Iran that has been politically unpopular and exacerbated the inflationary pressures facing everyday Americans. The CNBC Voter Poll found nearly three out of every four people said the war was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.
Trump told Fox News that voters were presumably unhappy with the surge in gas prices, even if they generally agreed with the need for military action against Iran. Vice President JD Vance said on social media that some voters who backed him and Trump in 2024 likely supported Democrats in the midterms as a result of the war.
U.S. drivers paid about $4.15 for an average gallon of gas on Tuesday, the highest of any midterm or presidential election day since at least 2000, according to AAA. Gas prices have surged about 37% over the past year as the Middle East conflict crippled the global crude trade.
"America sent a very clear message," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, a fuel price tracking platform. "Going into an election with prices that on Election Day have never been higher is something that garners a lot of frustration from consumers."
Higher prices for gas and other energy products have cost the average American household nearly $1,230 since the start of the Iran war, according to an analysis from Zandi. The financial pain felt by U.S. consumers from the conflict has spilled into other areas. Rising borrowing costs and expanded military services roughly cost households more than $900 in addition, according to Zandi.
The consumer price index, a broad basket of goods and services tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, reaccelerated during the war with Iran. Increases in consumer prices have outpaced wage gains in recent months, leaving consumers with less purchasing power.
Prices for diesel, the fuel type used by truckers and trains, climbed to records that transportation executives have said feel "like science fiction." In the latest producer price index report, the BLS said that rising diesel costs pushed up prices for many goods.
The CNBC Voter Poll found more than three out of every five people believed that Trump's policies led to higher prices. Almost nine out of 10 said they were very or somewhat concerned about the prices for a variety of goods such as utilities, food and oil. The poll was a collaborative effort across several news organizations that drew on about 100,000 interviews conducted by phone, online and in-person at polling locations with a margin of error of 0.6%.
Trump took over an economy coming out of the pandemic that was caught in a "vibecession," the term used to describe the disconnect between sour consumer confidence and positive economic fundamentals. With consumer prices now on one of their longest streaks of higher-than-preferred inflation readings on record, the average American's economic sentiment is even worse today.
The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey in 2026 fell to the worst levels in its seven-decade history. The Conference Board, meanwhile, said its consumer confidence gauge in September slid to 14-year lows.
Inflation pushed voters to a "breaking point," said Francesco D'Acunto, a Georgetown University professor who researches behavioral economics. "If consumers become angry voters, they vote against the status quo — in this case, the Trump administration."
Unpopular policies
Before the U.S. began its war with Iran in late February, economists and monetary policymakers were already sounding the alarm about what Trump's policies could mean for the economy.
Trump pitched his plan for broad and steep tariffs as a way to revive domestic manufacturing, but the policy sent financial markets reeling and raised the prospect of a potential recession. Researchers at the New York Federal Reserve said that many consumer prices would have fallen if not for Trump's tariffs, many of which were later struck down by the Supreme Court.
In the CNBC Voter Poll, 64% said Trump's tariff policies hurt the economy in their area. Just 14% said they helped.
Trump's White House also oversaw mass deportations in major cities that gave way to large-scale protests and the death of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents. A University of Pennsylvania study found that the cities experiencing immigration surges collectively saw decreasing foot traffic and billions of dollars in lost consumer spending.
About three out of five voters said they disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement handled its job and that the Trump administration had gone too far on the issue, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. Still, voters were more likely to say the Republican Party was better at handling immigration.
To be sure, some policies under Trump's White House have been better received. The Internal Revenue Service said in October that the average tax refund grew by 11% following the passage of Trump's "big beautiful bill." So-called Trump Accounts are allowing parents to tap into government and donor funds to build nest eggs for children.
But on Tuesday, voters showed that affordability remained a leading concern as the Iran war continues and inflation pinches pocketbooks. What changed compared with the 2024 presidential election was who they believed could fix it.
In 2024, more voters said they thought Trump was better equipped to handle the economy than former Vice President Kamala Harris. This week, voters said Democrats were better equipped than Republicans to handle the economy.
But the party will have a lot of work to do. Seven out of 10 respondents in the CNBC Voter Poll said they felt the U.S. economic system generally favored the wealthy.
"We know pretty clearly what is making Americans upset," said Zandi, who has advised politicians from both parties. "There's another election coming up in two years. Hopefully, policymakers are listening to all this."

articles.title: Qualcomm stock drops 7% on weak earnings forecast as memory shortage weighs on smartphone sales
articles.text:
Qualcomm reported quarterly results on Wednesday that topped Wall Street estimates, but the chipmaker's earnings forecast came in lighter than expected. The stock slid 7% in extended trading.
Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:
- EPS: $2.17 adjusted, versus $2.16 expected
- Revenue: $10.44 billion, adjusted
For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it sees earnings per share of between $2.15 and $2.35 on revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion. Analysts expected earnings per share of $2.27 on revenue of $10.48 billion.
Most of Qualcomm's chip sales come from system-on-chips and modems for smartphones. It's a market that's currently in turmoil as rising memory costs force handset makers to raise prices, hurting demand. Adjusted company revenue fell 7% during from a year earlier.
Qualcomm raised prices in September. Still, handset chip sales during the quarter fell 26% to $5.14 billion, trailing a StreetAccount estimate of $5.21 billion. Qualcomm said it's starting to see sequential growth in the category, and that Android shipments in China have bottomed, even though the company predicts the handset market will be flat in 2027.
Under CEO Cristiano Amon, Qualcomm has tried to turn investor attention to other kinds of chips. The company is looking to enter the fast-growing market for AI data center infrastructure. It had $650 million in data center revenue during the quarter, mostly from customizing and connectivity work, Amon said.
Amon said Qualcomm expects $5 billion in data center revenue in fiscal 2027. He said the company recently signed a customer for optical connectivity and had engaged a global hyperscaler.
"We don't have a demand issue; it's a supply issue," Amon said. "If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better."
Qualcomm also sells chips for cars and other automotive uses. Revenue in that division soared 89% on an annual basis to $1.99 billion, beating StreetAccount expectations of $1.66 billion.
Internet of things revenue includes low-power chips, smart glasses SoCs, laptop chips, as well as the company's bid to provide cellular infrastructure. Earlier on Wednesday, Qualcomm announced a deal to provide technology to SpaceX's cellular buidlout. IoT revenue increased 4% from a year earlier to $1.88 billion, slightly higher than estimates.
Qualcomm's QTL division includes revenue from licensing its intellectual property for 5G and other technologies to other companies. Qualcomm said during the quarter that it had renewed licensing agreements with Apple, Huawei, and Transsion.
"QTL will maintain its scale going forward," Amon said.
QTL revenue sank 7% to $1.3 billion, in line with a StreetAccount estimate.

articles.title: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
articles.text:
E.l.f. Beauty on Wednesday blew past Wall Street expectations as it posted a 51% increase in net sales in its second fiscal quarter.
The beauty company said it saw its 31st consecutive quarter of net sales growth, attributing the streak to strong performance across its portfolio. The revenue spike was driven by both retail and e-commerce channels across the U.S. and internationally, the company added.
"The thing I'm most pleased about is we saw strength across our entire portfolio," CEO Tarang Amin told CNBC in an interview. "Every one of our brands contributed strong growth this quarter."
Amin added that E.l.f. is the most-searched brand on TikTok Shop and the No. 2 brand in cosmetics on the platform. The company also said it saw strong results for Rhode, the skincare brand it acquired last year.
The company raised its full fiscal-year guidance following the better-than-anticipated quarter. It now expects net sales in the range of $2 billion to $2.03 billion, compared with a previous range of between $1.94 billion and $1.97 billion. It also upped its adjusted EBITDA projection to a range of $421 million to $427 million from between $401 million and $407 million.
E.l.f. said it now expects adjusted earnings per share for the year to come in between $3.82 and $3.86, exceeding prior guidance of between $3.50 and $3.55 per share. It's also expecting a net income range of $231 million to $233 million, up from a previous range of $212 million to $215 million.
It had already raised its guidance last quarter after outperforming its expectations.
Amin said the company is "very bullish" on the holiday season, expecting high sales through the end of the year.
Here's how the company performed in its second fiscal quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $1.21 adjusted vs. 60 cents expected
- Revenue: $520.8 million vs. $470.3 million
For the period ended Sept. 30, E.l.f. reported net income of $30.03 million, or 50 cents per share, up significantly from roughly $3 million, or 5 cents per share, the year prior.
Net sales grew 51% to $520.8 million.
E.l.f. also saw significant growth in its international channels, with business up 165%. Amin told CNBC that only 25% of the company's business is outside of the U.S. and that it has a "tremendous opportunity" to build on that momentum.
The company also said its gross margin increased 1.6% during the quarter, including a 0.3% benefit from tariff refunds. Amin previously said the retailer planned to fully reinvest that money into pricing and marketing to continue driving growth.
Though E.l.f. received most of its refunds in its first fiscal quarter, some of those funds flowed through the second quarter, and the company expects to receive a yearly total of around $55 million. Amin told CNBC on Wednesday that the company lowered the price of about 10% of its units by $1 because of the tariff benefits.
"We're seeing great unit momentum based on that," he said.

articles.title: What Democrats' midterm victory means for your crypto investments, according to experts
articles.text:
Democrats' takeover of Congress in the midterm elections could reshape efforts to regulate cryptocurrency, potentially bringing stronger investor protections while slowing legislation favored by the industry.
But everyday crypto investors shouldn't expect much to change immediately, experts tell CNBC Make It. Federal regulators appointed under President Donald Trump remain in place, and cryptocurrency trading will continue much as before.
"Platforms will keep offering the products they offer today, and they still have friendly regulators at the SEC and CFTC who are approving an ever-wider range of crypto products," says Lee Reiners, a cryptocurrency regulation expert and lecturing fellow of economics at Duke University.
The bigger question is whether lawmakers can agree on lasting rules for the industry — and how those rules could affect everyday investors.
What happens to the CLARITY Act?
The election results could further complicate efforts to pass the CLARITY Act, a bill intended to establish clearer federal rules for cryptocurrency trading.
The legislation would give the Commodity Futures Trading Commission greater authority over cryptocurrency trading while reducing the Securities and Exchange Commission's role in overseeing certain digital assets.
The distinction matters because the SEC generally regulates securities, such as stocks, and requires companies offering them to disclose financial information and investment risks. The CFTC primarily oversees derivatives markets, including futures contracts, and has more limited authority over everyday cryptocurrency trading.
The bill passed the House in July 2025 by a 294-134 vote, but failed to advance in the Senate in September 2026 on a 49-50 procedural vote. Democratic opponents argued the legislation could weaken investor protections by allowing some cryptocurrencies to avoid stricter SEC oversight, including disclosure requirements intended to help investors assess risk.
"CLARITY is dead," Reiners says. Although the bill could still pass during the lame-duck session before the new Congress takes office in January, he considers that unlikely.
Any future legislation would likely need to address Democrats' concerns about investor protections and conflicts of interest involving Trump's crypto businesses, says Martin Mulyadi, an accounting professor at Shenandoah University.
"The election does not end crypto market-structure legislation; it changes the authors of the next draft," Mulyadi says.
What does the election mean for crypto investors?
For everyday investors, the Democratic sweep is unlikely to change much about the cryptocurrencies they already own. But it could affect which new investment products become available, says Mike Katz, a digital assets specialist and financial services partner at law firm Manatt.
Newer crypto products, such as tokenized stocks and accounts that pay investors a yield on their cryptocurrency holdings, could face slower launches, additional restrictions or stronger investor protections as Democrats gain influence over crypto policy, he says.
With the midterm win, "the legislative agenda changes, oversight gets tougher and the assumption that Washington will keep making life easier for crypto becomes much harder to defend," says Katz.
That said, the SEC and CFTC can continue developing crypto regulations without Congress. But those rules could be reversed by future administrations, says Marcel Miu, a certified financial planner and founder of Simplify Wealth Planning.
"An agency's rules are much easier to reverse than laws, which is why the preferred pathway was the CLARITY Act," Miu says.
Even so, tighter regulation wouldn't necessarily mean lower cryptocurrency prices, says Evan Mills, a financial advisor at Scholar Advising. Prices will continue responding to interest rates, investor demand and other market forces. Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, was up nearly 3% Wednesday afternoon, trading above $80,000 following the Democrats' midterm victory.
"Investors should really not try to predict what Washington is going to do," Mills says. "They should spend more time on what they own, where they own it, how much exposure they have to this market and how much they're able to lose."

articles.title: Why we're kicking CVS out of our Bullpen watchlist. Plus, Intel's CEO makes a stand
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks jumped on Wednesday after the midterm elections, with the S & P 500 up about 1.7%. The elections turned out to be a clearing event for many parts of the market. WTI crude was down over 8%, falling below $90 per barrel, on hopes that the Democrats winning control of Congress means there won't be an escalation in the Middle East War. That pushed oil and gas stocks lower while lifting companies with exposure to energy commodities and the Middle East. There's also a view that the Democratic victory could lead to a rollback of tariffs, given how important affordability was to voters. Treasury yields also moved lower, with the benchmark 10-year yield dipping to 4.9%. The decline in oil prices, Treasury yields and tariff expectations provided a much-needed boost to housing-related stocks like Home Depot , which is back in positive territory for the year for the first time since August. Consumer staples and discretionary stocks also rallied on the idea that a drop in energy prices will provide a relief to consumer wallets, allowing for more spending at retailers like TJX Companies and coffee chains like Starbucks . Not everything was bought. Data center infrastructure stocks are getting hit hard on concerns that Democratic victories in the midterm elections could slow the pace of artificial intelligence data center construction, particularly in key markets such as Texas and Ohio. Since the end of the summer, we've cautioned around the growing political pressure against new data center construction into the midterms. We think the projects at risk are probably more "fringe" and "speculative" than those being undertaken by the major hyperscalers, but a slowdown in investment activity is negative for electrical equipment and power generation companies like Eaton and GE Vernova as well as the semiconductor stocks. Even AMD and Club name Qnity Electronics struggled despite both companies posting better-than-expected quarters with upbeat guidance. Intel shares continued their recent string of weakness, though the stock pared its losses after a filing showed CEO Lip Bu Tan purchased 150,000 shares on Monday at an average price of $64.73. It's good to see Tan show some conviction in the long-term Intel story after a disastrous 50% decline since the end of September. However, the purchase does not hold the same significance as it normally would because Tan — and us — incorrectly bought shares in the $90s in August when the company sold about $20 billion of stock . As AI capex beneficiaries faltered, the companies that have been funding the AI buildout — Amazon , Alphabet , Microsoft — were up big. Meta Platforms , another big spender, was slightly higher. The idea is that if new regulations limit data center development and force companies to slow their spending, their aggressive capital expenditure programs could be reined in, accelerating the timeline for free cash flow to inflect higher. Amazon, Alphabet and Meta have all sunk into negative FCF territory. Microsoft has remained positive, though its FCF has fallen over 20% year over year in back-to-back quarters. Slowing spending could also mean the hyperscalers won't need as many large debt and equity offerings to fund their buildout, which is something shareholders would embrace. Our take on the action Wednesday is that we don't want to overreact to some of these outsized moves in the AI trade – in both directions. If the data center buildout slows, it's not going to happen overnight. It's far too early to know how much of the anti-data center rhetoric will translate into actual policy and, by extension, affect companies' results. However, we would be ignoring the facts if we said some of the chip names and buildout stocks were as good of stories as they were last week. We're making one change to the Bullpen. We're taking out CVS Health , a name we added to our watchlist in early September alongside Kimberly-Clark , as we searched for more defensive ideas with cheap valuations and solid dividend yields. We liked CVS Health because the company was executing well under CEO David Joyner and the stock had recently pulled back on conservative 2027 earnings expectations. But the story changed on Wednesday, when the company announced plans to separate its national retail pharmacy from insurer Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager CVS Caremark. While there are merits to creating two independent companies, the process will take a very long time, with the breakup not expected to be completed until the first half of 2028. We're removing CVS Health from the Bullpen because the lengthy timeline could leave the stock stuck in "spin purgatory" until the breakup gets closer. Companies reporting after Wednesday's closing bell are McKesson , Qualcomm , Expedia , DoorDash , and Coherent . Before the opening bell on Thursday, we'll see earnings from Club names Kimberly-Clark and Cardinal Health . Also reporting are Cigna , Cummins , Parker Hannifin , Targa Resources , and Becton Dickinson . On the data side, we'll see the Labor Department's weekly jobless claims report and job cuts from the outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. articles.title: Loạt tàu chở dầu Nga sang Mỹ bất ngờ 'quay xe', chỉ còn 1 chiếc tiếp tục tiến về bờ Đông: Chuyện gì đang xảy ra?
articles.text:
Loạt tàu chở dầu Nga sang Mỹ bất ngờ 'quay xe', chỉ còn 1 chiếc tiếp tục tiến về bờ Đông: Chuyện gì đang xảy ra?
2 trong 3 tàu chở dầu diesel Nga từng hướng tới bờ Đông nước Mỹ đã thay đổi thông tin điểm đến, chỉ còn 1 tàu tiếp tục di chuyển.
Ngày 3/11, dẫn báo cáo của công ty theo dõi hàng hải Windward cho biết dữ liệu từ Hệ thống Nhận dạng Tự động (AIS) cho thấy hành trình của ba tàu chở diesel Nga đang có những thay đổi đáng chú ý. 2 tàu đã điều chỉnh thông tin điểm đến tự khai báo, làm xuất hiện khả năng kế hoạch đưa hàng tới các cảng Mỹ bị hủy hoặc các lô nhiên liệu sẽ được chuyển sang thị trường khác.
Trong số này, tàu Talisman mang cờ Nga trước đó hướng về khu vực Đại Tây Dương nhưng hiện chuyển trạng thái điểm đến sang chờ chỉ dẫn, không còn nêu khu vực cụ thể.
Tàu Leruo treo cờ Sierra Leone cũng thay đổi thông tin hành trình. Điểm đến mới được cập nhật theo hướng Brazil và ở trạng thái chờ chỉ dẫn. Diễn biến này cho thấy lô diesel trên tàu có khả năng được chuyển sang thị trường Nam Mỹ thay vì tiếp tục tới Mỹ như kế hoạch ban đầu.
Điểm chung đáng chú ý là cả Talisman và Leruo đều nằm trong các danh sách trừng phạt của Mỹ, Anh hoặc Liên minh châu Âu (EU). Tình trạng này tạo ra rủi ro pháp lý đáng kể đối với những bên tham gia giao dịch.
Nếu tiếp nhận các tàu nằm trong danh sách hạn chế, người mua, đơn vị vận hành cảng và các doanh nghiệp cung cấp dịch vụ hậu cần hàng hải có nguy cơ vi phạm quy định trừng phạt. Đây được xem là nguyên nhân chính khiến hai tàu phải điều chỉnh kế hoạch ban đầu.
Việc tàu thay đổi thông tin AIS không đồng nghĩa chắc chắn các lô hàng sẽ không tới Mỹ. Tuy nhiên, dữ liệu mới cho thấy kế hoạch vận chuyển diesel Nga sang thị trường này đang gặp nhiều trở ngại hơn dự kiến.
Trong 3 tàu được Windward theo dõi, Agioi Fanendes hiện là phương tiện duy nhất vẫn duy trì quỹ đạo thực tế hướng về vùng biển đông bắc nước Mỹ. Con tàu treo cờ Malta và thuộc sở hữu của một chủ tàu Hy Lạp. Agioi Fanendes cũng đã thay đổi thông tin cảng đến sang trạng thái chờ lệnh, song hướng di chuyển thực tế chưa thay đổi đáng kể.
Khác biệt quan trọng là Agioi Fanendes không nằm trong bất kỳ danh sách trừng phạt quốc tế nào được nguồn tin đề cập. Điều này giúp tàu tránh được một trong những rào cản pháp lý lớn mà hai phương tiện còn lại đang đối mặt.
Những thay đổi trên diễn ra sau khi Văn phòng Kiểm soát Tài sản Nước ngoài (OFAC) thuộc Bộ Tài chính Mỹ cấp phép nới lỏng một số giao dịch liên quan đến dầu mỏ, trong bối cảnh Washington tìm cách giảm sức ép thiếu hụt nhiên liệu trong nước. Động thái này mở ra khả năng diesel Nga được đưa tới Mỹ sau thời gian dài dòng chảy năng lượng trực tiếp giữa 2 nước bị gián đoạn.
Tuy nhiên, từ việc được cấp phép giao dịch đến khi một tàu chở nhiên liệu Nga thực sự cập cảng Mỹ vẫn tồn tại nhiều rào cản. Ngoài quy định của chính phủ liên bang, các bên tham gia một chuyến hàng còn phải tính tới tình trạng trừng phạt của tàu, chủ sở hữu, đơn vị vận chuyển và những tổ chức khác trong chuỗi giao dịch.
Diễn biến của Talisman và Leruo cho thấy những yếu tố này có thể trực tiếp ảnh hưởng tới quyết định thương mại và hành trình của các tàu. Đến ngày 3/11, chưa có lô nhiên liệu Nga nào trong nhóm này chính thức cập một cảng của Mỹ.
Theo Xinhua
